articles.title: Ashes ticket price increase 'really poor' - Vaughan
articles.summary: Former England captain Michael Vaughan is critical of a 43% ticket price increase for next year's men's Ashes Test at Edgbaston.
articles.body:
Former England captain Michael Vaughan has called a 43% ticket price increase for next year's men's Ashes Test at Edgbaston "really poor".

The Birmingham ground will host the third Test of the best-of-five series between England and Australia next summer with ticket prices in the Hollies Stand - which holds almost 6,000 spectators - costing £165, up from £115 in 2023.

Elsewhere in the stadium, members can purchase tickets for £92, but the cheapest adult tickets across the first three days are £115, with every ticket carrying a £2.50 booking fee.

"This is really poor," Vaughan posted on social media in response to the news.

Following the 2023 series, which ended in a 2-2 draw after Australia won the first two Tests (at Edgbaston and Lord's), the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) said "every day sold out in advance, with total attendance topping 545,000".

Despite Warwickshire's Edgbaston stadium being at a reduced capacity because of the construction of an on-site hotel, tickets for next week's third Test between England and Pakistan, which range between £57.50-£87.50 for adults, have not sold out.

The ticket ballot for the 2027 Ashes opened on Wednesday, with prices more expensive at Lord's and the Oval in London, with the best tickets at £190 and £185.

England, who lost 4-1 in Australia last winter, begin their quest to regain the Ashes at Trent Bridge in Nottingham on 18 June.

The second Ashes Test at Lord's begins on 30 June and the third at Edgbaston on 8 July.

The Utilita Bowl in Southampton will become the 10th UK ground to host a men's Ashes Test when the fourth Test gets under way on 21 July, with the series concluding at the Kia Oval from 29 July.

BBC Sport has contacted the ECB and the five Test venues for comment.

Ticket prices for sporting events have been an ongoing point of contention for fans.

A crowd of 13,623 were at Birmingham's 23,000-capacity Alexander Stadium to watch Britain's 24-year-old sprinter Amy Hunt win the women's 100m at the European Athletics Championships last month.

Athletics supporters blamed ticket prices, with Category A tickets for the home straight costing £150.

For the men's 100m final those same seats cost £110, again with no concessions for juniors.

In April, Ryder Cup organisers defended ticket prices for next year's centenary golf event between Europe and the United States in Ireland.

Daily general admission tickets for the three tournament days on 17-19 September at Adare Manor in County Limerick will cost 499 euros (£434), compared with up to 260 euros in Italy in 2023.

articles.title: Neeraj Chopra replaced by CWG bronze medallist Yashvir Singh as AFI announces 77-member squad for Asian Games
articles.summary: More sports News: Commonwealth Games bronze medallist javelin thrower Yashvir Singh has replaced injured Neeraj Chopra in India's athletics squad for the upcoming Asian.
articles.body: Commonwealth Games bronze medallist javelin thrower Yashvir Singh has replaced injured Neeraj Chopra in India's athletics squad for the upcoming Asian Games in Japan, while long-distance runner Abhishek Pal has been dropped after receiving a notice from the National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) over an alleged doping offence.The Athletics Federation of India (AFI) on Thursday announced a 77-member Indian track and field team for the September 19-October 4 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. The announcement was made during a press conference in Ludhiana, which is hosting the National Youth Championships.Men's 110m hurdler Tejas Shirse has also been left out of the squad after suffering an injury during the recent Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.AFI president Bahadur Singh Sagoo said Yashvir was brought in because Neeraj is unavailable due to injury."We have brought in Yashvir who is a CWG medal winner in place of Neeraj Chopra who is currently injured. It was an injury replacement and so there was no problem (in Yashvir coming in)," Sagoo said.He also confirmed that Abhishek Pal has been removed from the squad."Long distance runner Abhishek Pal has been dropped because of the issues he is facing. So this is the final team for the Asian Games," he added.Last month, Abhishek received a notice from NADA after his sample was found to contain a female fertility drug. Officials said the substance was present below the threshold level.Former AFI secretary and planning commission chief Lalit Bhanot said the federation did not want to take any risk while the investigation is ongoing."It's not a case of (Abhishek) returning dope positive. The presence of the substance is below threshold level. NADA is currently undergoing investigation. But we did not want to take any risk. We don't want anybody to point a finger on us. So, we have dropped Abhishek from the team," Bhanot said, as quoted by news agency PTI.Shirse and Abhishek were part of the 73-member squad announced by the sports ministry earlier this month. On Wednesday, the ministry added six more athletes to the athletics contingent.The six athletes added are Harita Bhadra (200m), Kiran Pahal (400m), Sindhushree G (pole vault), I Asha Ilango (triple jump), Sanya Yadav (discus throw) and Praveen Kumar (hammer throw).With two athletes dropped and six added, India's final athletics squad now has 77 members.The AFI has also requested permission for Avinash Sable to compete in the men's 5,000m in addition to his confirmed 3,000m steeplechase event.Sable, who won gold in the steeplechase and silver in the 5,000m at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games, has raced only once this season after recovering from ACL surgery."Sable's participation in 3000m steeplechase is confirmed, there is no problem in that. But we have also made a request to the Asian Games organisers for him to run in 5000m also."But, this is subject to him breaching the AFI qualification mark (in 5000m) during the final event of the Indian Athletics Series on September 10 in New Delhi," Bhanot said.The Indian Athletics Series Finals in New Delhi on September 10 will be a prize-money event, with most Asian Games-bound athletes expected to compete.The final squad also includes Gulveer Singh and Parul Chaudhary in three events each. Gulveer will compete in the 10,000m, 5,000m and 1,500m, while Parul will run the 3,000m steeplechase, 5,000m and 1,500m.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: American Olympics winner Tara Davis-Woodhall reveals she is ‘lucky to be alive’ after devastating crash
articles.summary: International Sports News: Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall has revealed that she is “lucky and blessed to be alive” after being involved in a serious car crash. T.
articles.body: Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall has revealed that she is “lucky and blessed to be alive” after being involved in a serious car crash. The American track and field star suffered a severe concussion after a head-on collision while driving to training last week. Both vehicles were badly damaged in the accident.The 27-year-old won long jump gold at the Paris Olympics 2024 and is now facing an uncertain period ahead of the World Athletics Ultimate Championship. Davis-Woodhall has not trained since the crash and said she is taking her recovery “day by day” after consulting doctors and physiotherapists.Tara Davis-Woodhall details scary car crash and training setbackTara Davis-Woodhall explained that the accident happened when she pulled into a parking lot while travelling at around 20mph. Another woman reportedly made a turn, resulting in the two vehicles crashing into each other.The impact was serious enough to write off both cars. Davis-Woodhall suffered a severe concussion but said she did not sustain any life-threatening injuries.“I pulled into the parking lot, and this lady just made a turn. We were both going about 20mph, so both of our cars were totalled. It’s very scary. I’m lucky and blessed to be alive and with no life-threatening injuries”, she said per The Sun.The accident has come at a difficult time for the Olympic champion. Davis-Woodhall was preparing for the World Athletics Ultimate Championship and believes she was in excellent form before the crash.The inaugural event is expected to bring together some of the biggest names in athletics. Winners of each event are set to receive a £111,000 prize ($150K).However, Davis-Woodhall’s participation is now uncertain. She has not returned to training since the accident.She has been working with doctors and physiotherapists to determine when she can safely resume her preparation.“I haven’t trained at all due to [the crash]. I’ve seen my doctors and my physios, and everyone’s just trying to get me back into it”, she added.Davis-Woodhall said she is physically recovering, but the accident has also affected her mentally.The timing has been especially frustrating for the American athlete. She said she was performing at the highest level of her career before the accident.“It’s really unfortunate timing. I’m at the peak of my training right now. I’m as fast as I’ve ever been. I’m as strong as I’ve ever been”, she discussed.Davis-Woodhall’s career-best long jump is 7.20 metres. She became one of the biggest stars in American athletics after winning Olympic gold in Paris in 2024.She is also known for her relationship with Paralympic champion Hunter Woodhall, whom she married. The couple have become prominent figures in track and field and have a large following.Davis-Woodhall most recently competed at the USATF Outdoor Championships in July. She finished third in both the long jump and the 100m hurdles.Her immediate focus is now recovery rather than competition. With the World Athletics Ultimate Championship approaching, she does not yet know whether she will be able to compete.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: Se impuso en la final del campeonato Master, que se disputa estos días en Daegu, con un tiempo de 1:25.33
articles.body: Pepi Sánchez Quintana sigue aumentando los éxitos en su palmarés. El último ha sido el oro que ha ganado en los 400 metros del Campeonato del Mundo de Master, que se disputa estos días en Daegu, a sus 76 años. La atleta andaluza se impuso en la final de la categoría, de F75, con un tiempo de 1:25.33, tras adelantar al esprint a la británica Roberts en los metros finales a la recta. articles.title: New Formula 1 Track Proposed as India Expands Motorsport Ambitions
articles.summary: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay has proposed a ‘Motor Sports City’ in his state along with Olympic City, to bolster the motor racing infrastructure,...
articles.body:
Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay has proposed a 'Motor Sports City' in his state along with Olympic City, to bolster the motor racing infrastructure, with an F1 track in mind.

While India's only F1 track Buddh International Circuit is looking for a revival in the coming years via new investment from Adani Group, Tamil Nadu CM Vijay has proposed a 'Motor Sports City' in his state to add and enhance the existing onto the motorsport culture.

He proposed the same during his speech in the Assembly on Thursday under Rule 110. Apart from other proposals, the Motor Sports City got an approval from India's first-ever F1 driver Narain Karthikeyan after he re-shared the speech on his Instagram handle.

No more details has been laid out by Vijay, but only a proposal to create a world-class facility that will not just house F1, but also the feeder competitions like Formula 2, Formula 3 and Formula 4. Basically, he wants to create a hub of racing in Tamil Nadu.

This will include race tracks and world class training facilities, to tap and develop young talent to compete at national and international levels in the time to come. Tamil Nadu already houses FIA Grade 2 & Grade 4 circuits in Chennai and Coimbatore, repsectively.

Both the Madras Motor Race Track in Chennai and Kari Motor Speedway in Coimbatore runs Indian national events and has hosted international events like F4 South East Asia and Asia Road Racing Championship (two-wheeler racing).

Vijay highlighted Tamil Nadu's leading capacity in production of four-wheel and two-wheel cars. In fact, the MMRT circuit is opposite to a huge Hyundai facility. Even for motor racing, he noted about key manufacturing units are based near KMS circuit.

He wants to tap on the potential and provide greater facilities for youngsters, whether as racers and or mechanics/engineers, to practice their skills and represent India at the larger stage. It is to be seen if the city will be an extension to Olympic City.

While the proposal is in place, it will be too early to jump on the F1 bandwagon just yet. Even the return of Indian GP to BIC seems like 2-3 years away while Adani Group battles out for ownership. There are positive indications, but still in discussions stage.

articles.title: Letsile Tebogo: Ultimate Championships provide emotional return to Budapest
articles.summary: Letsile Tebogo says his late mother is always with him "in spirit" as he prepares to run in Budapest, the city where she watched him make history for Botswana and Africa.
articles.body:
Olympic 200m champion Letsile Tebogo will return to Budapest for the Ultimate Championships next week, but the Hungarian capital is more than just another stop on the athletics calendar for the Botswana sprinter.

It is the city where the 23-year-old announced himself to the world and where his mother Seratiwa watched him make history for his country by claiming two medals at the 2023 World Championships.

This time Seratiwa will not be cheering on her son from the stands, having passed away in May 2024 after a short illness.

Having shared a close relationship with his mother - one she described as being more like a "brother and sister bond" - Tebogo admits that returning without her is difficult.

"I haven't really looked into the fact that I'm going now to Budapest without my mom," he said.

"It's just been a bumpy ride having to think about it and having to continue with the grind."

Three years ago, Seratiwa surprised her son by travelling to Budapest to watch the then 20-year-old compete in his first senior global championships.

Tebogo won silver in the 100m and bronze in the 200m - the first World Championship medals claimed by a male athlete from Botswana. He also became the first African man to win a World Championship medal in the 100m.

Seratiwa told BBC Sport Africa at the time that she was "proud" of what her son had achieved.

For all the memories the city holds, Tebogo says there is also a source of strength in returning to the place where his mother witnessed one of the defining moments of his career.

"I believe she's always there with me in spirit and in days where giving up is an option," he said.

"She pushes me to give my absolute best and I believe the memories that we had in Budapest, they will still come again."

African athletes need support and protection - Kebinatshipi

Botswana welcomes Tebogo home with stadium spectacular

Those memories now sit alongside everything that has happened since for Tebogo.

A year on from his success at the 2023 World Championships, Tebogo scaled greater heights by becoming Botswana's first Olympic champion when he won the 200m at the Paris 2024 Games, carrying his mother's initials on both his shoes and fingernails as a tribute.

He returns to Budapest as one of the faces of a new competition created to bring together the sport's best performers.

The Ultimate Championships is a biennial global event designed to crown the best of the best in a track and field season.

The three-day end-of-season competition includes Olympic champions, world champions, Diamond League winners and the year's other leading performers.

The inaugural edition in Budapest, which runs from 11-13 September, has a $10m (£7.41m) prize pot - the highest in track and field history according to organisers World Athletics - with each gold medallist taking home $150,000 (£111,000).

Tebogo, who helped Botswana to gold in the 4x400m at the World Relays on home soil earlier this year before registering 200m wins at the Diamond League events in Oslo and Lausanne, says the 200m in Budapest will not only be about looking back.

He is one of the team captains for the Kids' Athletics Ultimate Challenge, where young people from across the city will be invited to participate in activities at the Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre the day before the Ultimate Championships begin.

That will give him the chance to share some of the lessons he has learned since first stepping onto the global stage.

"I believe firstly you should start with accountability," he said.

"Think about your preparation, how you want your journey or your season to be, and then also think of unwavering sportsmanship.

"I would love them to have that unwavering sportsmanship, so that they can share lanes, they can cheer for one another."

articles.title: From a below-average shooter to Olympic gold-winning coach: How Jelena Arunovic brought a new energy to India’s shooting camp
articles.summary: More sports News: In a parallel world, Jelena Arunovic could be a time traveller. One moment, the pistol coach could be seen reading a newspaper, scanning it thoroughly.
articles.body: In a parallel world, Jelena Arunovic could be a time traveller. One moment, the pistol coach could be seen reading a newspaper, scanning it thoroughly, making her shooters do it too. In the next, she could be sneakily taking photos to upload on her ‘insta’ stories.While reading newspapers probably make her one of the most aware persons in the Indian shooting setup, her selfies allow her to bond with the shooters, who train with her for hours, every day at the national camp in Bhopal.The shooter-turned-coach is bringing in a new energy, and it is contagious. She is breaking norms by becoming a cheerleader, friend to the shooters, while also maintaining her stature as pistol shooting coach.The Serbian has come to India after successfully coaching her sister Zorana and Damir Mikec to 10m air pistol mixed team gold at the Paris Games. After her stint with the Serbian national team, Jelena worked as the head coach of Guangdong Province in China.“I have some experience with Asian teams — last year, I was in China — but this is completely different. Everything is more intense, not just with the national team but in general, from food to everything else. So far, I like it,” Jelena, 45, told TOI.The Serbian is getting used to India’s way of over-reaction. “Everything is very emotional. The intensity is five times bigger when we are sad, when we are happy, when we celebrate. Everything is over the top. When we are happy, we are very happy. When we are sad, it’s the end of the world. I’m still adapting,” she confessed.“I’m still trying to find similarities with the Serbian national team and with Chinese athletes and trying to change myself also so I can fit in better and give better results,” she said.Jelena participated in world competitions from 1997 to 2012, she took up coaching after retiring from active shooting. On how the two experiences were different, the Serb said both her roles are incomparable. “These experiences are completely different. As an athlete, I was below average. I have only one medal, a silver from the World Championships in Olympic disciplines. I never mention that because I think it’s rude to mention my personal experience when you have such a good group of athletes. How can they relate to one medal from the World Championships?” she admitted.“But as a coach, my experience is on a completely different level. I have won everything. That is the thing that I'm the proudest of, because I know how difficult it was for me and my sister, to be patient, believe in our work and be good enough to win that Olympic gold medal,” she said.“I understood very early that I cannot compare with the best athletes. I was very honest and said ‘this will not work’ although I was very persistent. My abilities were not at the desired level. Then I said, ‘Okay, I like this sport. My sister was very talented back then. I think I will try to be a coach’," Jelena said about her journey.While the younger sister is preparing herself for the Los Angeles Olympics, the elder sister is training her competitors in India. “We laugh about it. She would have wanted me with her, but she understands my professional commitments and is very proud of what I have been doing.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

Additionally, 110m hurdler Tejas Shirse was ruled out due to foot stress fractures suffered during CWG.These two exclusions offset the latest addition of six athletes — Harita Bhadra (200m), Kiran Pahal (400m), Sindhushree G (pole vault), I Asha Ilango (triple jump), Sanya Yadav (discus), and Praveen Kumar (hammer throw) — who were cleared by the ministry after the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) accepted IOA’s late request for their addition, bringing the count from 73 to 79 before Pal and Shirse’s omissions brought the contingent size down to 77.AFI is also seeking approval for Hangzhou double-medallist Avinash Sable to compete in the 5,000m alongside his confirmed 3,000m steeplechase event. However, Sable must first breach the AFI qualification mark of 13:39.18s at the Indian Athletics Series Finals here on Sept 10, where most Asian Games-bound athletes will compete.Know Yashvir-- Born in Devsar, Haryana and raised in Jaipur, Raj.-- Shifted from basketball to javelin at age 13, initially practicing with bamboo javelins.-- Coached by his father Rai Singh, a former Indian Railways national champion.-- Broke Chopra’s U-20 Federation Cup record in 2021; joined the 80m club in 2022 (82.13m).-- Overcame major shoulder surgery in late 2023 that kept him out for nearly a year.-- Claimed bronze at Glasgow CWG with a final-throw personal best of 85.41m.-- Became only the third Indian male javelin medallist in CWG history after Kashinath Naik and Chopra.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Jonny Brownlee retires from triathlon at 36
articles.summary: Jonny Brownlee, a former Olympic triathlon champion and six-time world champion, says "it's over for professional sport".
articles.body:
Former world and Olympic champion Jonny Brownlee has retired at the age of 36.

The Briton won Olympic bronze at London 2012, silver at Rio 2016 and gold in the mixed relay at Tokyo 2020.

He is also a six‑time world champion and won mixed team relay gold at the 2014 Commonwealth Games.

Brother Alistair, a double Olympic champion, retired at the age of 36 in 2024.

"I've been thinking about it for a while. I've won more than I ever thought I'd ever achieve," Jonny told BBC Sport.

"One thing I'm really proud of is we full on committed to winning Olympic medals and delivering our best performance. And now I just don't think I can do that any more.

"It's over for professional sport, but I don't think you ever truly stop."

Brownlee said the birth of his son Freddie 10 months ago clarified his plans for the future.

"I don't think I can have that commitment because of how life is. He's my priority now, my family, but also with my body as well," said Brownlee.

"The thought of missing a training session used to be the worst thing in the world, whereas now, if Freddie is ill or needs me, then without question I do that.

"I used to have absolutely no fear with racing. I used to dive into corners on my bike at 60kph and not care.

"If I hit that corner and crash, then I can't hold Freddie for five to six weeks if I have got a broken wrist. I was asking if that was really worth it any more."

In a glittering career, Brownlee said the moments that resonate most are London 2012 and the World Series coming to his home city of Leeds in 2016.

"To deliver those medals [in 2012] was something I'm incredibly proud of," he said.

"The first time racing in Leeds kind of symbolised everything, the whole journey.

"The fact that there was a World Series in Leeds was just unthinkable when we started triathlon, and then to come into the Millennium Square for the first time was one of the proudest moments of my life and something I'll never forget."

Brownlee said sharing such a long career alongside Alistair was "unbelievably special", but that the famous 2016 World Series Triathlon race in Mexico played on his mind.

Jonny was leading when his legs started to give way on the run leg in gruelling heat.

Alistair, who was in third at the time, propped Jonny up for the final 700m and helped him over the line.

"It really annoyed me at the start. I've got multiple Olympic medals, world championships - and that got remembered," said Brownlee.

"Quite often now people say 'Which one are you? Are you the one who did the carrying or the one who got carried?' So yeah, it does grate me a little bit."

However, Brownlee said he is "proud" of the moment and that it underlined the importance of helping others.

Brownlee said he knew there was one medal left to claim before he stepped away - an Olympic gold.

Brownlee said he "committed everything" and "used my last bits of energy" to take mixed triathlon gold alongside Jessica Learmonth, Georgia Taylor-Brown and Alex Yee at the Tokyo Olympics.

"If I hadn't won that Olympic gold medal I think there would always be something missing," he said.

He said winning gold was the moment he was "finally known as Jonny Brownlee, and not as the person who came 10, 15 seconds behind Alistair".

"I'm incredibly proud that we've had an impact on the sport," he said.

"It's time to move on because I wouldn't be doing myself justice by doing it half-heartedly any more.

"Although they are saying I'm retiring from professional racing, I'm definitely not stopping the sport. If anything, I'm actually going to race more."

"Quite often now people say 'Which one are you? Are you the one who did the carrying or the one who got carried?' So yeah, it does grate me a little bit."

However, Brownlee said he is "proud" of the moment and that it underlined the importance of helping others.

Brownlee said he knew there was one medal left to claim before he stepped away - an Olympic gold.

Brownlee said he "committed everything" and "used my last bits of energy" to take mixed triathlon gold alongside Jessica Learmonth, Georgia Taylor-Brown and Alex Yee at the Tokyo Olympics.

"If I hadn't won that Olympic gold medal I think there would always be something missing," he said.

He said winning gold was the moment he was "finally known as Jonny Brownlee, and not as the person who came 10, 15 seconds behind Alistair".

"I'm incredibly proud that we've had an impact on the sport," he said.

"It's time to move on because I wouldn't be doing myself justice by doing it half-heartedly any more.

"Although they are saying I'm retiring from professional racing, I'm definitely not stopping the sport. If anything, I'm actually going to race more."

articles.title: Caitlin Clark, Paige Bueckers lead Team USA to strong win over China in debuts at 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup
articles.summary: The veterans got Team USA a lead Friday and the youngsters closed it out with authority.
articles.body:
All the pressure is on Team USA at the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup. After winning the event four straight times, that's now the expectation for newcomers like Paige Bueckers and Caitlin Clark.

In their first test as a team, the U.S. proved it was more than capable, defeating China 94-61 on Friday. In the process, Clark and Bueckers showed they are more than ready to represent Team USA.

It was a mostly smooth ride for Team USA, which led by roughly 20 points for the majority of the contest. On the offensive side, Jackie Young and Rhyne Howard led the way for the Americans early before Clark and Bueckers finished late. Young, who started the contest, finished with 12 points and three assists in the victory. Howard, who came off the bench, helped the team build its lead early, finishing with 14 points.

For all of Team USA's excellence Friday, there was one moment in the contest where the U.S. hit resistance. In the second quarter, China went on an 11-3 run after switching to a zone defense. During a halftime interview, Team USA coach Kara Lawson admitted that China's defense "stymied" her team briefly.

But Team USA found its way through that wall, eventually taking a 20-point lead into halftime. It was able to push that lead in the second half.

With the game in hand, the reserves saw more time in the third and fourth quarters and did not disappoint. After a quiet first half, Bueckers came alive late, finishing with 14 points, her first of which came after a smooth steal.

Clark also made her presence felt, though not as a scorer initially. During the first half, Clark acted as a distributor, racking up assists and finding the open player. Once Team USA shifted to its youth lineup in the second half, Clark started firing up shots, eventually tying for the team lead in points.

Along the way, she managed to hit one of her patented, long-range 3s.

She also continued shelling out assists, eventually securing a double-double (14 points, 11 assists) in her first-ever FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup game.

Angel Reese did her usual thing, playing relentless defense and pulling down rebounds. She finished with five points and eight rebounds in the win.

By the end of the contest, every single member of Team USA scored. Sonia Citron — another member of the team's youth movement — was the last to secure a bucket, finishing with two points.

It was a play that perfectly encapsulated why Team USA is going to be a problem for its opposition at the event.

It was an encouraging debut from that group, and from the team generally. While that was always the expectation, the team did hit some adversity Monday, when it was announced A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum would not play in the event due to injury .

Additionally, China wasn't necessarily going to be an easy win, as the team met the U.S. in the championship during the 2022 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup.

Despite all that, Team USA took care of business Friday. In the process, they proved why they are the favorites to once again win it all. The veterans played as expected, while the youngsters proved they were more than ready for the limelight.

Team USA will look to carry that momentum into its next game in the event, which will come against Italy on Sunday.

articles.title: El Barça gana al Porto y defenderá su título en la final de la Supercopa Ibérica
articles.standfirst: Triunfo relativamente plácido pese a la reacción del equipo luso en la segunda parte
articles.summary: Triunfo relativamente plácido pese a la reacción del equipo luso en la segunda parte
articles.body: El Barça cumplió los pronósticos y se clasificó sin mayores dificultades para la final de la Supercopa Ibérica después de doblegar al FC Porto (39-37), en un partido en el que los azulgranas mostraron su superioridad desde el inicio del duelo. Antonio Carlos Ortega apostó de inicio por situar a Janus Smárason, fichado del Pick Szeged, junto a los franceses Dika Mem y Timothey N'Guessan en la primera línea. Al islandés y a Peter Cikusa le tocará esta temporada asumir muchos minutos en ataque tras la marcha de Domen Makuc al Kiel. Con un juego eléctrico, rápidas transiciones y un gran trabajo defensivo, el Barça golpeó al Porto con un parcial 7-1 en seis minutos. Carlos Martingo, técnico portugués, paró el encuentro (10-4, min.10). Su equipo mejoró en ataque con la entrada de Xabi Barbosa y Joao Gomes, pero el Barça alcanzó el intermedio jugando con rentas de seis y siete goles (22-15, descanso). Una relajación del vigente campeón de Europa y ganador de las cuatro anteriores ediciones de la Supercopa Ibérica, tres goles seguidos del lateral islandés Thorsteinn Gunnarsson y la escasa aportación de su compatriota Viktor Hallgrímsson en la portería del Barça apretaron el marcador en el arranque del segundo tiempo (24-21, min.33). El Porto, que esta temporada competirá en la Liga de Campeones, empezó a soñar con una épica remontada, pero la mejoría defensiva del Barça enterró sus opciones de sorpresa (30-26, 33-28, 36-32). En el minuto 55, con 37-33 en el marcador, un codazo de Miguel Oliveira en la cara de Peter Cikusa provocó el enfado del banquillo azulgrana, llegando Antonio Carlos Ortega a encararse con el entrenador portugués. 39 Barça: Hallgrímsson, Dani Fernández (6,2p), N´Guessan (1), Smárason (3), Dika Mem (6), Frade (5) y Aleix Gómez (5,3p) -equipo titular- Novakovic (ps, 1gol), Ludovic Fábregas, Djorde Cikusa (2), Carlsborgard (2), Blanz Janc, Elderaa , Adrián Sola (1), Peter Cikusa (1), Ian Barrufet (6, 2p) y Oriol San Felipe. 37 FC Porto: Abrahamsson, Pedro Oliveira (3), Miguel Oliveira (4), Gilberto Duarte, Persson (2), Brandao (3) y Antonio Martínez (6,4p) -equipo titular- Rui Silva (1), Joao Gomes (3), Xavi Barbosa (4), Guilherme Borges (6), José Ferreira, Pedro Antunes (ps), Leonel Fernandes, Vasco Costa (2) y Gunnarsson (3). Marcador cada cinco minutos: 5-3, 8-4, 12-7, 16-9, 18-13, 22-15 (descanso); 25-22, 28-24, 32-27, 34-31, 37-33 y 39-37. Árbitros: Alberto Murillo Castro y Pablo García Sánchez (comité andaluz). Mostraron tarjeta roja directa al portugués Miguel Oliveira (min.55) por un codazo en la cara a Peter Cikusa. Además, excluyeron a Peter Cikusa por parte del Barça, y a Vasco Costa, Borges, Giberto Duarte, Joao Gomes y Brandao por parte del FC Porto. Incidencias: Encuentro correspondiente a la primera semifinal de la Supercopa Ibérica masculina de balonmano disputada en el IFEVI de Vigo ante unos 1.300 espectadores.

articles.title: No Duplantis, no party: se retira por lesión y desluce el primer día de las finales de la Diamond League
articles.standfirst: Recae de sus molestias musculares y deja incluso en el aire su presencia en el Ultimate Championship, el nuevo campeonato de World Athletics, la próxima semana en Budapest
articles.summary: Recae de sus molestias musculares y deja incluso en el aire su presencia en el Ultimate Championship, el nuevo campeonato de World Athletics, la próxima semana en Budapest
articles.body: Las finales de la Diamond League 2026, el histórico Memorial Van Damme en el Estadio Rey Balduino de Bruselas -que cumple su quincuagésima edición-, no han tenido el comienzo deseado, entre otras cosas porque el gran duelo del día se ha frustrado antes de empezar por culpa de una lesión. Porque la gran noticia de la primera jornada fue la renuncia de Armand Duplantis a saltar tras sentir molestias musculares en el calentamiento. El rey de la pértiga ya se había retirado de una competición el pasado 18 de julio en Londres aunque en aquella ocasión sí había realizado varios saltos. Ese día, 'Mondo' sintió que sus molestias en el muslo izquierdo iban a más -de hecho compitió con un fuerte vendaje en esa pierna- y, tras hablarlo con su padre, decidió retirarse del concurso. Era su segunda derrota en una temporada atípica que veremos cómo acaba, pues es la gran referencia del Ultimate Championship, la competición de nuevo cuño de World Athletics que se estrena el próximo fin de semana en Budapest. "Es terrible. Este problema en la pierna empezó en Londres. Desde entonces, todo iba bastante bien y trabajé muy duro, pero el dolor volvió en Zúrich. Seguí adelante de todos modos, probablemente demasiado. Me dije a mí mismo que si sentía esa molestia durante el calentamiento, no saltaría. Así que tomé la difícil decisión de no competir", diría luego el bicampeón olímpico en zona mixta. "Lo peor que podría pasar es tener que retirarme a mitad de la competición. Los aficionados querían ver un gran espectáculo y me habría encantado dárselo. Desafortunadamente, ahora mismo no puedo. Tengo la cabeza hecha un lío. Es extremadamente difícil, pero así es la vida de un atleta. Intento mantener la calma y ser positivo. Veremos si puedo participar en el Ultimate Championship. Todavía no tengo la respuesta”, añadió el genio nórdico. La baja del sueco abría la puerta de par en par a Emmanouil Karalis, el atleta griego que venía de superar los 6,20 metros en Zúrich y se había atrevido a abordar el récord mundial (6,32) en presencia de su rival y amigo. 'Manolo' recogió el guante y ganó sin oposición con un gran salto de 6,12 metros -el noruego Sondre Guttormsen, segundo, se quedó en 5,82-, récord del meeting en detrimento del propio Duplantis. La otra gran final de esta primera jornada, al menos a priori, era la masculina de 1.500 metros, más que nada por la presencia del corajudo Jakob Ingebrigtsen, que buscaba una segunda victoria de prestigio tras su triunfo en el 5.000 del Europeo de Birmingham. El noruego se fue tras las liebres desde la primera vuelta y entró primero a la recta de llegada pero ahora mismo no tiene el 'punch' necesario en una prueba tan exigente como el 'milqui' y acabó siendo superado por el australiano y chico de moda Cameron Myers (3:30.14) y el keniano Phanuel Koech (3:30.18). Ingebrigtsen acabó perdiendo incluso la tercera plaza en beneficio del americano Ethan Strand (3:30.50) pese a tirarse sobre la misma línea de meta (3:30.52), lo que refleja su indomable espíritu competitivo. La sorpresa negativa fue la séptima plaza del campeón olímpico Cole Hocker (3:30.80). Otra gran carrera era la masculina de 800 metros, con todos los gallos del corral en liza. El esloveno Jan Vukovic ejerció a la perfección de liebre -paso el 400 en 49.58- y dejó todo en manos del campeón olímpico Emmanuel Wanyonyi. El keniano hizo una carrera limpia, sin toques, y fue abriendo hueco para acabar ganando con un tiempo de 1:41.80, récord del meeting y casi un segundo menos que el argelino Djamel Sedjati (1:42.71). También cumplió con su papel de favorito el estadounidense Ja’Kobe Tharp, nuevo plusmarquista mundial de los 110 vallas, que volvió a flirtear con la barrera de los 13 segundos para imponerse con un registro de 13.03 (-0.2). En el peso femenino, precisamente la primera de las 32 finales que se van a disputar entre hoy y mañana, triunfo de la estadounidense y bicampeona mundial Chase Jackson con 21,14 metros, récord de la Diamond League y segunda mejor marca mundial en lo que va de siglo, sólo por detrás de los 21,24 de la mítica Valerie Adams. En la longitud masculina, 'sorpasso' del jamaicano Tajay Gayle, que con un último vuelo de 8,46 (+1.4) metros relegó a la segunda plaza al griego y gran favorito Miltiadis Tentoglou con 8,40 (+0.5). También hubo un desenlace inesperado en el disco femenino, con la china Feng Bin alcanzando los 67,46 metros y evitando el sexto triunfo de la estadounidense Valarie Sion en las finales del circuito pese a un último intento de 66,92 metros. El vigente campeón mundial de los 100 metros, el jamaicano Oblique Seville, logró su primer diamante pese a una mala salida, remontando en el último tramo de carrera para acabar con un crono de 9.90 (+0.1). Por lo demás, destacar la victoria del esloveno Kristjan Ceh en el disco con un gran mejor lanzamiento de 71,29, superando al lituano y plusmarquista mundial Mykolas Alekna (70,14), y los incontestables triunfos de la santalucense Julien Alfred y el botsuano Busang Kebinatshipi en los 200 y 400 metros respectivamente con dos 'marcones': 21.79 (+0.1) y 43.40, marca personal y récord de la Diamond League.

articles.title: Diamond League results: Amy Hunt continues strong season with third in Diamond League final
articles.summary: Amy Hunt's strong late-season form showed no signs of letting up as she clocked a season's best to finish third in the 200m at the Diamond League final in Brussels.
articles.body:
Amy Hunt's strong late-season form showed no signs of letting up as she clocked a season's best 22.16 seconds, just eight hundredths off her lifetime best, to finish third in 200m at the Diamond League final in Brussels.

The Briton, who picked up four gold medals at the European Championships in Birmingham last month, was beaten by St Lucia's Julien Alfred, the fastest women over the distance this year, who took victory in 21.79, and American Kayla White in 22.00.

"I'm really really proud of that one," Hunt told BBC World Service.

"That was probably one of the best bends I've ever done, if not the best. I could feel I was so close to Julian, then the long season kind of caught out to me in the last 20 metres."

A third-place finish continues Hunt's upward trajectory in the finale of the 15-stop elite circuit.

She came fifth and sixth respectively in the 2025 and 2024 Diamond League finals over 200m.

Hunt will also run in the 100m event on Saturday night, drawn alongside American Olympic silver medallist Sha'Carri Richardson, and intends to similarly double up at the inaugural Ultimate Championships event in Budapest, which begin on 11 September.

"We train over 400 metres and the longest recovery we have in winter sessions is 45 seconds," added Hunt.

"I'm out there doing the really long reps back to back to back and that's enabling me to do this really packed schedule."

Hunt finished furthest up the results list of any of the Britons in action.

Matt Hudson-Smith was fifth in the 400m, well off Botswana's world champion Collen Kebinatshipi, while Jake Hayward, running in his Wales vest, was eighth in a captivating 1500m race.

Australian 20-year-old Cameron Myers expertly picked a path to victory, edging out Kenyan teenager Phanuel Koech. Their rivalry could play out over plenty more big stages in the future.

Elsewhere, world champion Oblique Seville took the 100m in 9.90 seconds and Kenya's Emmanuel Wanyonyi won his fourth successive Diamond League title over 800m.

After Sweden's Armand 'Mondo' Duplantis opted not to compete in the pole vault final after feeling tightness in his leg, his Greek rival Emmanouil Karalis, who has climbed to second in the event's all-time list this year, took centre stage and victory with a 6.12m clearance.

While Duplantis is doubt for the all-star Ultimate Championships event, one of its biggest names will definitely be missing from the startlists after Olympic 100m champion Noah Lyles announced an injury-enforced early end to his season.

articles.title: Amy Hunt: British sprinter runs season's best 200m time to take third in Diamond League Athletics meet in Brussels
articles.summary: Amy Hunt runs 22.16 in Brussels, her best 200m time of the season; Sweden's pole vault world record-holder Armand Duplantis withdraws with back tightness, a week before the inaugural World ‌Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest; Noah Lyles ends season early due to injury
articles.body:
Hunt's time of 22.16 was outstripped by race winner - and reigning Olympic 100m champion - Julien Alfred of St Lucia (21.79) and America's Kayla White (22.00).

Another Brit, Success Eduan, came seventh of the eight runners after clocking 23.06 in Belgium.

Hunt was the poster girl of the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham this summer with her four gold medals and bubbly personality winning her legions of fans.

The 24-year-old topped the podium individually in the 100m and 200m in the Midlands, while she won gold as part of the women's and mixed 4x100m relays.

Elsewhere in Brussels on Friday night, European 400m men's gold medalist Matthew Hudson-Smith, of Great Britain, finished fifth in his event.

Duplantis in injury scare ahead of World Athletics Ultimate Championships

Sweden's pole vault world record-holder Armand Duplantis was forced to pull out of the Diamond League final with back tightness, a week before the inaugural World ‌Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest.

Duplantis said: "The worst possible thing to do is having to pull out of a competition. The fans wanted to see a good show and I wish I could deliver that. Unfortunately, I can't right now.

"My head is everywhere right now. It's super difficult, but that's life, that's the life of an athlete. I try to stay calm and positive. We will see if I can make the Ultimate Championships. I don't have the answer right now."

The World Athletics Ultimate Championships is a new biennial event which sees world champions, Olympic champions, Diamond League winners and other leading athletes compete against each other for shares of a $10m (£7.87m) purse.

Each individual ​champion will secure $150,000 (£110,865), the biggest winner's ​cheque in track and field history.

Noah Lyles, the men's 100m champion at the 2024 Paris Olympics, will not take part, having ended his season early due to injury - but he still plans to travel to Hungary.

"I am still ​going to be at Ultimate Championship. I still do have ​parties to throw and things to do behind the scenes to help support ​the athletes," Lyles said.

"I still think that this is going to be an ⁠amazing competition, and I'm excited to watch that. And I'm even more excited to see what the future is going to bring."

articles.title: Atletas citam frustração com maratona suspensa pouco antes da largada | G1
articles.standfirst: Prefeitura de Piracicaba (SP) diz que suspendeu prova após análises técnicas apontarem irregularidades no percurso.
articles.summary: Prefeitura de Piracicaba (SP) diz que suspendeu prova após análises técnicas apontarem irregularidades no percurso.
articles.body:
Edição anterior da Maratona Internacional de Piracicaba — Foto: Prefeitura de Piracicaba

A organização da Maratona Internacional de Piracicaba (SP) já apresentava falhas mesmo antes de ser suspensa pela prefeitura pouco antes da largada , no último dia 30 de agosto. É o que afirmou ao g1 a educadora física Verônica Fraga, que assessora dez alunos que participariam da corrida.

A Secretaria de Esportes, Lazer e Atividades Motoras informou que a suspensão ocorreu após análises técnicas apontarem irregularidades no percurso que poderiam acarretar em risco de acidentes para os atletas.

"A gente via que era um evento que estava deixando a desejar por algumas coisas. Desde quando começou a anunciar a prova, não tinha um local onde estava o percurso. Você entrava no site onde estavam as inscrições, não tinha o percurso. Tinha o regulamento, mas não tinha nada do percurso. A gente pedia informações, o pessoal não respondia às mensagens que a gente mandava", afirma Fraga.

Ao todo, atletas de quatro países e 190 cidades estavam confirmados na competição, que havia começado no sábado (29) com a realização da corrida infantil e as provas de cinco e dez quilômetros. Já no dia seguinte, aconteceriam as etapas de 21 e 42 quilômetros. Ambas foram suspensas.

A atleta Jaqueline Martins Cipriano participaria da maratona e destacou a frustração diante da suspensão.

A atleta Jaqueline Martins Cipriano participaria da Maratona Internacional de Piracicaba — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

"Essa corrida estava no meu ciclo de preparação para a próxima maratona. Então é uma frustração. O que a gente faz é fazer um replanejamento e uma solidariedade muito grande porque eu estava acompanhando vários atletas amigos que iam estrear na maratona e na meia maratona, então, para mim, é mais o problema do replanejamento, mas, com os meus amigos que iam estrear, é decepção, é frustração", cita.

Cipriano ainda reforçou a ausência de informações prévias sobre o percurso da prova.

"Todos os meus amigos que estavam tentando buscar ali informações de percurso informações de local de hidratação, de ponto de hidratação, de banheiro, que são coisas que são relevantes para quem vai. Não tinha resposta não tinha nenhum tipo de retorno da organização."

William Cordeiro, que também atuaria, observou uma mudança na organização do trânsito em relação a outras provas que participou.

"Normalmente, quando você chega à prova, uma hora antes, já está tudo fechado. Então, assim, o trânsito está fechado, às vezes você quer parar em um lugar, você tem que dar a volta na cidade pra parar no lugar que você determina. E ali estava o trânsito rolando normal", pontuou.

Segundo a Secretaria de Esportes, foram identificadas as seguintes irregularidades:

Ausência ou deficiência na implantação das interdições;

Falta de sinalização e dispositivos de canalização em pontos previstos;

Ausência de equipes de apoio (staff) que deveriam estar posicionadas ao longo do percurso.

Ainda de acordo com a pasta, a organização da prova foi comunicada para adoção das providências necessárias para regularizar a situação, mas que as falhas não foram corrigidas.

A prefeitura também ressaltou que a realização de corridas de rua promovidas por empresas ou entidades privadas é de responsabilidade da própria organizadora do evento. Já a prefeitura atua na análise, autorização e apoio institucional ou operacional.

"A Administração lamenta ainda os transtornos causados aos participantes e à população, mas reforça que a segurança das pessoas é prioridade e deve prevalecer sobre a realização de qualquer evento", afirmou.

A Grécia Produções e Eventos , responsável pela organização da prova, disse que estão sendo realizadas tratativas para definir se haverá uma nova data para a realização da prova e que, somente após essa definição, será possível estabelecer os procedimentos relacionados a inscrições e eventuais devoluções.

A empresa informou que comunicou previamente à sociedade as informações sobre a prova, por meio de faixas e materiais de sinalização instalados nas vias.

Citou, ainda, que o fechamento das vias estava autorizado pelo órgão competente de trânsito para ocorrer somente 30 minutos antes da largada, às 3h30.

"É importante esclarecer também que, em uma corrida de rua, existem diferentes tipos de operação viária. Algumas vias são compartilhadas entre atletas e veículos, com a utilização de cones, cavaletes, grades e faixas para garantir a segurança e a organização do percurso. Outras são interditadas exclusivamente para a circulação dos atletas", complementou.

A Federação Paulista de Atletismo (FPA) , por sua vez, garantiu que a competição encontrava-se com toda organização técnica em linha com as melhores práticas de corrida de rua realizadas no estado de São Paulo e informou que acompanha a situação para prestar o suporte necessário para solução do caso.

"A Federação Paulista de Atletismo realizou contato com a empresa organizadora do evento e o fará também com a Prefeitura Municipal de Piracicaba, para ampla apuração dos fatos e compreender, detalhadamente, todas as razões administrativas e técnicas que levaram ao embargo da prova, e dar suporte para adequada solução do caso", completou.

articles.title: Jonny Brownlee's early years remembered as triathlete retires
articles.summary: A Jonny Brownlee retires, former coaches and teachers recall his and brother Alistair's impact.
articles.body:
Those were the words of triathlete Jonny Brownlee, who announced his retirement from professional sport on Friday, aged 36.

Now the Olympian is taking a step back from the starting line, former coaches, teachers and those inspired by his success have spoken about his legacy.

The younger Brownlee brother is a six-time world champion, and won gold, silver and bronze medals from the Olympic Games.

He and older brother Alistair, who twice won Olympic triathlon gold, grew up in the Leeds suburb of Horsforth, and both still live locally.

They were members of several sports clubs as children, including Bingley Harriers, and still have strong relationships with those they met there.

Their impact on triathlon, both locally, and beyond, can still be felt today, according to swimming teacher and the pair's former coach Coz Tantrum.

"They've got Yorkshire heart and they've got Yorkshire grit," she said.

Tantrum coached Jonny and Alistair from the ages of 11 and 13 respectively, when they joined the City of Bradford swimming club. Their early lessons in the pool were at Aireborough Leisure Centre in Guiseley.

Even from a young age, the brothers were committed to all three disciplines of the triathlon, Tantrum explained, although Jonny was the more "relaxed" of the pair.

"I'd finish the session and they'd literally sprint out of the pool and into the changing rooms.

"You'd see them outside handing the kit off to their parents and off they'd go, and they'd be running home or biking home."

Tantrum continued to coach the brothers until December last year, and witnessed first-hand their many successes and how they pushed each other, and the sport, on.

"They've got a massive amount of loyalty towards each other," she said.

For her, this was encapsulated when, in 2016, Alistair helped an exhausted Jonny over the line at the Triathlon World Series in Mexico .

"I think that's the moment when they became more than the triathlon brand.

"They transcended the triathlon, they transcended the sport, and there's not many people that can say they do that."

In the corner of Tantrum's swimming academy, she has a cabinet of Brownlee memorabilia to inspire others.

"If kids are getting into triathlon, everybody talks about them," she said.

"They have completely transformed triathlon. It's not just the legacy that they've left for Yorkshire, it's the legacy that they left for Great Britain."

PE teacher Matt Wilde taught all three Brownlee brothers at Bradford Grammar School - the youngest, Ed, is now a vet. Jonny also played team sports there, including rugby and cricket.

They were "incredibly intelligent, focused and ambitious" in their academic studies and sporting pursuits, he recalled.

"Bradford Grammar School is incredibly proud. They have inspired and still continue to inspire the pupils here."

Teaching alongside colleagues Tony Kingham, who ran the school running club, and Michael McCartney, Wilde said he felt "very fortunate" to play a small part in their lives.

The Old Bradfordians often return to their former school, to support the mini-triathlon event it holds annually, in association with the Brownlee Foundation.

The charity works with educational centres and other partners to introduce children to active lifestyles through all three triathlon sports.

Wilde added that although the pair are "superstars" it still felt "very normal" to see them back on school grounds.

"They are history makers but they're just well-grounded, normal individuals who have achieved such a huge amount in the world of triathlon," he said.

There are others in the region that had more fleeting, yet just as memorable, encounters with the Brownlees.

Back in 2012, organisers at York Parkrun were astonished to see Jonny - on the cusp of his first Olympic medal - turn up to take part in the weekly 5km event.

One of the volunteers that day said the young athlete turned up with "no fuss, no entourage".

"The story goes that he had been up studying all night and decided to come out and stretch his legs at York Parkrun," they said.

The course record in 2012 was 15 minutes and 57 seconds which Jonny comfortably bested with 14:43. It stood until 2017.

The volunteer added that "as a relatively new Parkrun and being in the lead-up to the 2012 Olympics, his visit did give us a lot of pride".

For their entire careers, the brothers used training facilities at the University of Leeds, where Jonny also studied history.

Even their kit requirements were met locally, as they were regular customers at triathlon specialists Triangle in Guiseley.

The late owner Adam Nevins, who died in a motorcycle accident in 2023, gave them advice on equipment when they were first entering races as children.

The Brownlee Centre, a collaboration between the university and Leeds Beckett, is the first purpose-built triathlon training centre in the UK.

Rhys Davey, head of triathlon at the centre, spent many years training alongside the brothers, having first met them at university.

He described their commitment to training as "immense" from the very beginning.

"Not only are buildings named after them and a cycle track, but they really have inspired a generation of young people to do triathlon.

"They are a huge part of the reason [the centre] has grown to where it is today."

Pete Mackreth, dean of Carnegie School of Sport at Leeds Beckett, said the university congratulated Jonny "on an incredible career full of medals and memorable moments".

After the retirement of Alistair in 2024, Jonny's decision brings the curtain down on the Brownlee era of triathlon and their contribution to the sport entering the mainstream.

Mackreth added: "He's contributed to securing an incredible legacy for triathlon in the UK and in Leeds, helping to make the city a global centre of excellence in the sport," he said.

"I am sure Jonny will continue his long relationship with Leeds Beckett, and hope he remains a regular on campus whatever he decides to do next."

articles.title: Hugo González brilla en Brasil con cinco oros y el récord de España de 100 estilos
articles.standfirst: El reciente subcampeón europeo de los 200 estilos muestra su poderío en el campeonato brasileño de piscina corta
articles.summary: El reciente subcampeón europeo de los 200 estilos muestra su poderíó en el campeonato brasileño de piscina corta
articles.body: Hugo González está de dulce. Tras su medalla de plata en los 200 estilos del Europeo de París, con la sexta mejor marca de todos los tiempos, acaba de cerrar de forma brillante su participación en el Campeonato de Brasil de piscina corta. Se marcha de la competición con siete medallas (cinco oros) y el récord de España de los 100 estilos. González, con familia brasileña por parte materna, se tomó esta competición con una opción más de lograr tiempos por debajo de las mínimas exigidas para el Mundial de noviembre en Pekín por si pudieran ser consideradas por la Federación aunque no sea una prueba selectiva a nivel nacional. Hugo cerró su participación con el oro en los 100 estilos que vino unido a la nueva plusmarca nacional. Nadó en 51.46 (muy por debajo de los 52.39 que se exigirá en el Nacional de Madrid de noviembre para ir al citado Mundial y de los 52.56 que poseía como marca personal) y batió el récord en posesión de Carles Coll desde que paró el crono en 51.50 en el campeonato del Mundo de 2024. Antes había ganado también los 200 espalda (1:49.84, marca personal y por debajo de la mínima mundialista), los 200 estilos (1:52.75. también menos tiempo que la mínina), 400 estilos (4:03.24, mínima) y 100 espalda (50.62, marca personal). Fue segundo en los 200 braza (2:03.54, marca personal y mínima) y tercero en los 50 espalda (23.53, marca personal).

articles.standfirst: El noruego, cuarto en la final de 1.500 de la Liga de Diamante, cuestionó la elección final de las liebres, una de ellas compañero de Hocker, que no mantuvieron el ritmo previsto
articles.summary: El noruego, cuarto en la final de 1.500 de la Liga de Diamante, cuestionó la elección final de las liebres, una de ellas compañero de Hocker, que no mantuvieron el ritmo previsto
articles.body: Pese a que hizo su mejor marca de la temporada en 1.500 (3:30.52), una distancia para la que aún le falta rodaje, Jakob Ingebrigtsen finalizó muy enfadado tras correr la final de la distancia en la Liga de Diamante, en la que acabó cuarto por detrás del victorioso Cameron Myers. El noruego criticó la elección de las liebres, una de las cuales fue reemplazada por un compañero de entrenamientos de Cole Hocker, que no mantuvo, según su versión, los ritmos previstos. "Intentamos ganar (,,,), pero nos engañó en cuanto a seguir el ritmo. Quizás estaba enfermo o lesionado, o simplemente no tuvo un buen día". Durante la carrera, primero Jackson y después Kiprugut, mantuvieron un ritmo más lento del que se había marcado. De hecho, en la final se vio a Ingebrigtsen intentando acelerar y superar al keniata, que se vio obligado a salir de la carrera para que el grupo avivara el ritmo. Por eso, Jakob se mostró "muy decepcionado con la carrera y el resultado, estoy compitiendo contra un montón de cobardes. Así son las cosas". El noruego insistió en que "solo Cameron [Myers] es un buen corredor, todos los demás parecían perdedores, yo incluido".

articles.title: Werro se lleva la 'batalla' del 800 ante Bol en un duelo que amenaza la historia
articles.standfirst: La suiza suma su segundo diamante en Bruselas tras ganar a Femke por seis centésimas, en una jornada con grandes marcas y récords del mitin
articles.summary: La suiza suma su segundo diamante en Bruselas tras ganar a Femke por seis centésimas, en una jornada con grandes marcas y récords del mitin
articles.body: Con permiso de la británica Keely Hodgkinson, ausente en las últimas citas de Liga de Diamante por molestias físicas, dos mujeres, Audrey Werro y Femke Bol, han situado el 800 femenino en el primer foco del atletismo mundial. Sus duelos, pese a que la neerlandesa apenas lleva un año en esta distancia a la que llegó tras ganarlo casi todo en los 400 metros vallas, empiezan a escribir páginas que se avecinan históricas en los próximos años. Porque la suiza, única atleta de siempre en bajar en tres ocasiones de 1:54.00, ha corrido este año en 1:53.70, tras hacerlo previamente en 1:53.98, el que se erigió en el mejor tiempo en la distancia en 18 años hasta que ella misma lo ha mejorado. Y poco a poco se va acercando al récord de Kratochvilova, el más antiguo del atletismo (1:53.28). No dio otro paso más hacia esa plusmarca este sábado, en Bruselas, en una carrera que, sin embargo, dejó de nuevo un majestuoso duelo entre la suiza y Bol. Tras el disparo, Werro se situó tras la liebre, con el objetivo de no dejar opciones de maniobra a la neerlandesa en los metros finales. Bol, sin embargo, siguió la estela de la suiza y a punto estuvo de superarla antes de meta. Pero Audrey sumó el diamante, con 1:54.75, récord del mitin, que tenía Pamela Jelimo desde 2008, por delante de la exvallista, que acabó segunda, con 1:54.81. Este fue uno de los múltiples récords del mitin que llegaron en esta segunda jornada de finales de la Liga de Diamante, que se disputó en el Estadio Rey Balduino de Bruselas. El último de ellos llegó en los 400 metros vallas masculinos, que pusieron el broche a la jornada. Sin Warholm en liza, tras desavenencias económicas con la organización, el brasileño Dos Santos, plusmarquista mundial, firmó otra apabullante victoria, con 46.70, por delante del estadounidense Bassitt (48.03). La dominicana Marileidy Paulino refrendó con otra victoria su gran dominio en los 400 metros en 2026. La campeona olímpica de la distancia se impuso de nuevo con gran solvencia y sumó así su sexta victoria en Liga de Diamante este año, todas por debajo de 49.00, esta vez con 48.64, récord del mitin (que tenía Richards-Ross, con 48.83). La noruega Jaeger acabó segunda, con 49.20. Con una gran salida (0.139), y una excelente aceleración en los primeros pasos, la jamaicana Tina Clayton se adjudicó su primer diamante en los 100 metros a sus 22 años. Lo hizo con un registro de 10.93, la única de las finalistas en bajar de 11.00. Segunda fue la reina de la velocidad europea este año, la británica Amy Hunt, con 11.06, mientras que la estadounidense Sha'Carri Richardson completó el podio (11.07). Previamente, en una carrera de 100 Invitational, Jael Bestué fue tercera, con 11.28. En los 5.000 metros, el bareiní Birhanu Balew lanzó un espectacular ataque, incontestable para sus rivales, a falta de 400 metros para ganar su primer diamante con un gran registro de 12:45.70, récord de Asia, además de mejor marca mundial del año. Ntakarutimana, de Burundi, cruzó tras él la meta, en 12:46.73, récord nacional. No tuvo rivales Kenneth Bednarek en el doble hectómetro. El estadounidense estuvo desde el inicio en cabeza y aguantó sin problemas para sumar otro diamante a su palmarés, al ganar los 200 metros en un gran registro de 19.62, con el que igualó su propia marca al frente del ranking del año. El sudafricano Dambile fue segundo, con 19.89. Y Tebogo, campeón olímpico, sólo pudo ser cuarto, con 20.01. Con una gran Lorea Ibarzabal en sus prestaciones de liebre, la polaca Klaudia Kazimierska dio la sorpresa y se impuso en unos fulgurantes 1.500 femeninos, con 3:54.05, récord nacional y del mitin, marca que le permitió también situarse líder mundial del año. La keniata Ewoi fue segunda, con 3:54.72. En los 3.000 obstáculos, el etíope Godana volvió a superar a El Bakkali, como ya hizo en Silesia, con un ataque en la contrarrecta al que el marroquí no pudo responder. Godana sumó su primer diamante, con 8:08.67, por delante de El Bakkali (8:10.03). Por su parte, el único español en liza en estas finales de Liga de Diamante, Dani Arce, acabó quinto, con 8:14.03, tras una valiente carrera. Una de las grandes marcas de la jornada llegó en el peso, en el que se impuso el jamaicano Rajindra Campbell, que se hizo así con su primer diamante. Aunque ya había batido el récord nacional en su segundo intento, con 22,62, el gran registro llegó en su sexta tentativa, en la que lanzó la bola hasta los 23,08 metros, de nuevo plusmarca de Jamaica, récord del mitin y cuarta mejor marca de siempre. Hacía más de dos años que no se lanzaba tanto, desde que Ryan Crouser batiera el récord del mundo en Los Angeles, con 23,56 en mayo de 2023. Tras Campbell, completaron el podio de esta final de Liga de Diamante los estadounidenses Jordan Geist, con 22,23, y Joe Kovacs (22,09). En la jabalina femenina, el triunfo fue para la china Ziyi Yan, que se impuso con un lanzamiento de 68,42, en su quinto intento, un registro que supone récord del mitin, que tenía hasta este sábado Kara Winger, con 68,11. Con 18 años, 3 meses y 14 días, se convirtió en la atleta más joven en ganar un diamante. Mientras, en el foso del triple, el italiano Andy Díaz brincó hasta los 17,74 metros (récord del mitin) en su primer salto, suficiente para desnivelar a su favor el duelo con el portugués Pichardo, que fue segundo, con 17,51. En la pértiga femenina, Hana Mall hizo marca persona, 4,91, para adjudicarse el diamante, mientras en la longitud femenina, su compatriota Monae Nichols hizo lo propio, con 6,91. Por último, en la jabalina masculina, la victoria fue para Pathirage, de Sri Lanka, con 89,04.

articles.title: Diamond League Final 2026: Amy Hunt 'not afraid of anyone' after second-placed 100m finish
articles.summary: Amy Hunt says she is "on the up" and "not afraid of anyone" after finishing second in the 100m at the Diamond League final in Brussels.
articles.body:
Amy Hunt says she is "on the up" and "not afraid of anyone" after finishing second in the 100m at the Diamond League final in Brussels.

The 24-year-old Briton finished in 11.06 seconds, behind Jamaica's Tina Clayton who won in 10.93, just one day after a third-placed finish in the 200m.

Hunt's performance surpassed American Olympic silver medallist Sha'Carri Richardson, who came third in 11.07.

It continues Hunt's fine late season form after winning four gold medals at the European Championships in Birmingham last month.

"I am 24 and on the up and up and up. I am not afraid of the other girls," said Hunt.

"I have so much love and respect for them and they are absolute icons but I love the challenge of going head to head with them.

"It takes me back to younger days racing boys in the school playground."

Hunt is planning to compete in the 100m and 200m again at the inaugural Ultimate Championships event in Budapest, which begins on 11 September.

"To come away with two podiums is no mean feat, and I am the only athlete to double up in the sprints and I came away with a second and a third," added Hunt.

Fellow Briton Georgia Hunter Bell came fourth in the 1500m despite being among the pre-race favourites.

Hunter Bell has won three international titles this year, including the world indoor 1500m, Commonwealth Games 800m and European 1500m, but never looked like threatening the top three in Brussels.

Poland's Klaudia Kazimierska came first with a time of three minutes 54.05 seconds, with Kenya's Dorcus Ewoi second and Australia's Jessica Hull third.

Hunter Bell said her performance was a result of a "long hard season", with the 32-year-old having competed in 19 races this year.

"I have done three championships so I am starting to feel it in my body," said Hunter Bell.

"I am struggling a little bit, even mentally to get my adrenaline up again week in, week out, but I am really lucky to be racing and to be happy and healthy.

"I just have to regroup before the Ultimate Championships next week, but I have to be happy with my consistency this season."

Elsewhere, Switzerland's Audrey Werro won the women's 800m final but was pushed all the way by Dutch athlete Femke Broeders-Bol.

With British Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson missing through injury, Werro hung on during the final straight with Broeders-Bol at her heels.

Werro, who has set the third, fourth and fifth fastest 800m times in history this year, finished in 1:54.75, which was 0.06secs in front of Broeders-Bol.

Brazil's Alison dos Santos and America's Masai Russell, who set world records in the men's 400m hurdles and women's 100m hurdles last week respectively, repeated their victories in Brussels but could not better the times they set in Zurich.

articles.title: Taylor crowns career in stylish Croke Park triumph
articles.summary: Katie Taylor ends illustrious career as a three-time undisputed world champion as Croke Park gave one of Ireland's greatest sporting figures the grandest of...
articles.body:
Katie Taylor ended her illustrious career as a three-time undisputed world champion as Croke Park gave one of Ireland's greatest sporting figures the grandest of farewells on a night of celebration, spectacle and music.

The 40-year-old outclassed unbeaten Flora Pili on points in front of 80,000 jubilant fans to add the vacant WBC belt to her WBA, WBO and IBF light-welterweight titles.

With the footwork, speed and sharp pressure fighting that defined her career, Taylor produced one final stylish performance against the overmatched Frenchwoman to win by scores of 110-90, 110-90 and 98-91.

After almost a quarter of a century in the sport, Taylor - an Olympic champion, two-weight world champion and one of the pioneers of women's professional boxing - finally got her fairytale ending at her dream venue.

She bows out with a record of 26 wins and just one defeat, but this was about more than one final result.

It was a night steeped in Irish pride, with a spine-tingling atmosphere and chart-topping pop group Westlife helping provide a fitting send-off.

On an unforgettable night for the city, around 80 per cent of those inside Croke Park had never previously attended a boxing event, but turned out to honour a fighter who dragged women's sport from the margins and took an entire nation on her journey.

The crowd was the sixth largest recorded post-war attendance for a boxing event anywhere in the world. By early evening, the stands were awash with green and white, tricolours draped over shoulders.

Westlife performed 'World of Our Own' and 'You Raise Me Up', with tens of thousands joining in as phone lights flickered around the towering tiers of Croke Park.

The atmosphere softened for an a cappella version of 'Grace', the well-known Irish ballad linked to the 1916 Easter Rising, before the national anthem rang out.

Chants of "Ole, Ole, Ole" drowned out Pili's ring-walk music before Taylor finally emerged to 'All Hail King Jesus', a nod to the faith she has spoken so openly about throughout her career.

She stretched her arms wide, sang along and tried to take in every second of her final walk to the ring. There was emotion on her face, but also the familiar focus as fireworks shot into the Dublin sky.

Taylor had spent fight week insisting there was still a job to do, but even for a fighter who had sold out Madison Square Garden and performed on some of boxing's grandest stages, it was hard to imagine her being untouched by a reception like this.

After a quiet opener, Taylor - Olympic champion at London 2012 and a professional since 2016 - burst into life in the second round, firing quick combinations before darting back out of range.

She repeatedly beat Pili to the punch, working in bursts and making the most of the two-minute rounds.

Pili, 29, arrived unbeaten in 12 contests and had previously held the European title. With little expectation on her shoulders, she had everything to gain.

But she had never faced anyone remotely close to Taylor's level and the gulf in class soon began to show.

The party atmosphere continued between rounds as it became increasingly clear there would be no gatecrashing from the Frenchwoman.

Former world champion Prince Naseem Hamed and UFC star Paddy Pimblett watched from ringside as Pili swung wildly in the fifth, only for Taylor to make her miss and fire back.

Pili enjoyed her best spell in the seventh, a quick flurry briefly snapping Taylor's head back, but it did little to alter the direction of the fight.

Croke Park rose for the final two minutes as Taylor continued to press forward, letting her hands go while the noise poured down from the stands.

She embraced her mother, trainer and manager in the ring as 'Celebration' rang around Croke Park before the inevitable result was read out.

"Let me just look around for a second", she said afterwards, soaking up every ounce of the reception.

articles.title: Rumesh Pathirage makes history with stunning 89.04m throw to win Diamond League Final
articles.summary: More sports News: Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage capped a remarkable 2026 season by becoming the first athlete from his country to win the men’s javelin throw ti.
articles.body: Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage capped a remarkable 2026 season by becoming the first athlete from his country to win the men’s javelin throw title at the Diamond League Final in Brussels on Saturday.Making his debut at the prestigious season-ending event, the 23-year-old produced a winning throw of 89.04m in the third round at the King Baudouin Stadium. The effort came after a relatively quiet start but proved enough to secure the title.“I’m truly very happy about that,” Rumesh said. “Coming from a small country like Sri Lanka, winning a major meet like this.”Pathirage opened the competition with throws of 80.42m and 79.73m, falling well short of the distances he had regularly produced throughout the season. Trinidad and Tobago’s former Olympic champion Keshorn Walcott initially took charge with 83.99m, before Poland’s Dawid Wegner produced a huge personal best of 87.47m in the third round to move into first place.Pathirage responded later in the same round.His 89.04m effort immediately restored him to the top of the standings and ultimately proved decisive.The Sri Lankan followed his winning throw with efforts of 85.96m and 85.76m before fouling his final attempt. Wegner could not better his third-round mark, leaving Pathirage with a winning margin of 1.57m.Pathirage overcomes difficult conditionsPathirage admitted that the conditions in Brussels made it difficult to reproduce the enormous distances he had been achieving during the season.“Honestly, I couldn’t get a big throw today because the weather conditions were quite difficult - it was very cold... so that’s why I couldn’t reach a big distance,” he explained.Wegner took silver with his 87.47m personal best, while Walcott completed the podium with his season-best 83.99m.Grenada’s two-time world champion Anderson Peters finished fourth with 83.70m. Peters moved close to Walcott with his fifth-round throw, but the latter held on to third by just 29cm.Kenya’s former world champion Julius Yego finished fifth with 76.79m, followed by Belgium’s Timothy Herman on 71.79m and American Curtis Thompson on 69.52m.Second major title of breakthrough seasonThe Diamond League crown is Pathirage’s second major title of the season after he won Commonwealth Games gold in Glasgow, finishing ahead of India’s former Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra.His triumph in Brussels also capped an extraordinary Diamond League campaign.Pathirage won four meetings during the season and finished runner-up in another. His victories came in Rome, Doha, Lausanne and Zurich, while he finished second at the Silesia Diamond League.His biggest performance came in Rome in June, where he produced a Sri Lankan national record and world-leading throw of 92.62m.He subsequently won in Doha with 88.68m and Lausanne with 88.14m before ending his Diamond League regular-season campaign with another massive effort of 92.07m in Zurich.Pathirage has therefore become the only javelin thrower to cross the 92m mark twice this season. He also owns eight of the top 10 throws in the world in 2026 and currently sits at No. 1 in the world rankings.Neeraj Chopra absence adds intrigue to Asian GamesPathirage’s historic Diamond League triumph comes just days before the Asian Games, where he will have another major challenge ahead.India’s Neeraj Chopra has withdrawn from the Asian Games after being ruled out with injury, leaving Pathirage set to face Olympic champion Arshad Nadeem, Commonwealth Games bronze medallist Yashvir Singh and prominent Indian thrower Rohit Yadav.The men’s javelin qualification is scheduled for September 26, with the final set for September 28.With the Asian Games and the World Ultimate Athletics title still to come, Pathirage now has the chance to add further silverware to what has already been one of the most dominant seasons of his young career.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Asian Games: Step by step, Avinash Sable rebuilds the belief
articles.summary: More sports News: BENGALURU: For 14 months, Avinash Sable has been fighting a battle that has had little to do with the stopwatch. At the Monaco Diamond League in July .
articles.body: BENGALURU: For 14 months, Avinash Sable has been fighting a battle that has had little to do with the stopwatch. At the Monaco Diamond League in July last year, the 2023 Asian Games steeplechase champion stumbled over the water jump after a competitor ahead of him lost balance. Sable went down too, limped off the track and into the longest injury layoff of his career.Surgery for a torn ACL and meniscus forced the 31-year-old to miss the Glasgow Commonwealth Games and begin the long, often lonely grind to recovery. There was high-altitude training in Ooty, a stint at the Inspire Institute of Sport in Bellary and, more recently, preparation at the SAI South Centre in Bengaluru.“The past year was very difficult for me because since my steeplechase debut in 2017, this is the longest I’ve stayed away from competition,” Sable said.The Monaco injury was particularly cruel because it came when he was in the form of his life. In May last year, Sable had won gold at the Asian Athletics Championships in Gumi, South Korea, clocking a season-best 8:20.92. “That medal gave me the confidence to aim higher. During the period when I won the Asian medal, my fitness was at its best. So, I thought I would do my personal best at the Monaco Diamond League, and then the injury happened,” he rued.He has since managed to put the setbacks behind him. “For the Asian Games, I started training continuously from June, and I’m feeling good and confident,” he said.The first test of that confidence comes at the Indian Athletics Final Series in New Delhi on Sept 10, when Sable will make his return to competition. “I will build my confidence at the event and do better than the last Asian Games,” he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
