articles.title: Ricardo Ten sigue abonado al podio: subcampeón mundial de contrarreloj en Huntsville
articles.standfirst: Segunda medalla de España tras la plata de Manuela Vos en la jornada inaugural. Damián Ramos se ha quedado a diez segundos del podio en la clase C4
articles.summary: Segunda medalla de España tras la plata de Manuela Vos en la jornada inaugural. Damián Ramos se ha quedado a diez segundos del podio en la clase C4
articles.body: Ricardo Ten sigue agrandando su leyenda como deportista y en la segunda jornada del campeonato del Mundo en Huntsville (Alabama, Estados Unidos) ha conquistado la plata mundial en la contrarreloj C1, lo que supone la segunda medalla -y la segunda plata- para la delegación española tras la de Manuela Vos en la jornada inaugural. El valenciano ha completado los 14,6 kilómetros de competición en 20:03.87, registro que le ha permitido asegurarse la medalla de plata. Ten ha quedado a 33,87 segundos del oro, que ha sido para el francés Thomas Tarou con un tiempo de 19:30.00. El estadounidense Aaron Keith fue bronce (20:11.10). Desde su debut mundialista en 2017, cuando el valenciano cambió la natación por el ciclismo tras dos décadas de éxitos, suma 36 medallas mundiales: 20 oros, 10 platas y 6 bronces entre pista y carretera. Por su parte, Damián Ramos rozó la medalla en la categoría C4. Acabó quinto la contrarreloj con un tiempo de 36:39.67 en los 29,2 kilómetros, a tan solo 10,46 segundos de la medalla de bronce. El francés Gatien Le Rousseau se llevó el oro y Kevin Le Cunff y Mattis Lebeau, completaron un podio cien por cien francés. En el tándem masculino, las dos parejas españolas han terminado entre las cinco mejores del mundo. Joan Sansó y Eloy Teruel fueron cuartos, con 33:48.70, a 1:16 del bronce, mientras que Imanol Arriortua y Mikel Aristi han sido quintos con 33:56.66. La victoria ha correspondido a los franceses Elie de Carvalho y Mickaël Guichard, por delante de los neerlandeses Tristan Bangma y Patrick Bos y de los también franceses Alexandre Lloveras y Thomas Denis. En C3 masculina, Juan Alberto Jiménez y Eduardo Santas han estado dentro del Top-6. Jiménez ha finalizado quinto con 38:21.17, mientras que Santas ha ocupado la sexta plaza con 38:44.32. El joven francés Louis Hubert ha conquistado el arcoíris con 36:03.41, seguido por los canadienses Michael Sametz y Alexandre Hayward. La categoría C2 masculina ha dejado la duodécima posición de Maurice Eckhard, que ha marcado 20:24.41 en los 14,6 kilómetros; mientras que en la prueba femenina C2, Verónica Rodríguez ha terminado también en octava posición con un registro de 24:47.41.

articles.title: Eilish McColgan wins fourth London Big Half after five-month injury lay-off
articles.summary: Britain's Eilish McColgan returns to competitive action after five months out with a fractured foot to win the London Big Half for a fourth time.
articles.body:
Eilish McColgan claimed her fourth victory at the Big Half in London on Sunday after returning to action following five months out with a fractured foot.

The 35-year-old Scot suffered the injury during the London Marathon in April, crossing the line in seventh place with blood seeping through her shoe, and was forced to pull out of July's Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

But McColgan showed the benefit of months of warm weather training, completing a comfortable victory over the 13.1-mile course back in the English capital.

The British women's half-marathon record holder beat last year's winner Jessica Warner-Judd by one minute 19 seconds, finishing in a time of 1hr 10mins 54secs.

McColgan might have 'one more' Games in her

McColgan to miss Glasgow Games defence after foot fracture

It was more than three minutes outside her best time for the course and well outside her British record for the distance of 1:05:43.

Britain's Jack Rowe missed out on a record fourth consecutive victory in the men's race, finishing in second place, 14 seconds behind Birchfield Harriers' Kadar Omar Abdullahi, who won in a time of 1:01:51.

Britain's David Weir defended his title in the men's wheelchair event, winning the race for the fifth time in its nine-year history in a new record time.

The 47-year-old, who retired from Paralympic competition in 2024, knocked 45 seconds off his own record for the course, which he set last year, winning in 46:13.

Eden Rainbow Cooper won the women's event in 52:47 to defend her title.

articles.title: Figure skating icon Nancy Kerrigan offers local tutorial, talks Alysa Liu
articles.summary: Kerrigan spoke with The Desert Sun about her ongoing passion for figure skating, her views on today’s Olympic stars and her impressions of the valley.
articles.body:
On an unusually rainy day in the Coachella Valley, two-time Olympic medalist Nancy Kerrigan offered insights to local skaters during a tutorial at the Berger Foundation Iceplex at Acrisure Arena.

The clinic held Sunday, Sept. 6, was open to skaters of all ages and skill levels, and it cost $275 to participate, or $250 for members of the Desert Figure Skating Club . Some came from as far as Ontario and Pasadena to spend time with the famous figure skater, who won a bronze medal at the 1992 Winter Olympics and a silver in 1994.

Kerrigan was also at the center of a bizarre, infamous incident in January 1994, when she was struck on her knee by an assailant with a police baton who later turned out to be the ex-husband of her rival, Tonya Harding. Kerrigan quickly recovered and still competed in the Olympics weeks later.

Before putting on her skates and showing some moves to those gathered at the Berger Foundation Iceplex, Kerrigan sat down with The Desert Sun to briefly talk about her passion for the sport, her perspective on today's Olympic stars like Alysa Liu and her impressions of the valley. Here is what the figure skating Hall of Famer had to say.

Olympian Nancy Kerrigan hosts figure skating workshop at Iceplex

Q: Why do you think it's important to hold events like this and put on these kinds of tutorials?

A: I love doing the camps because it just brings these communities of skaters together and it is a strong community. No matter what rink I go in, it feels like home kind of. They're just people doing the same thing I love to do, so it's a nice opportunity to share my too many years (laughs) of practice and knowledge. I feel honored that I get asked to share that and help in some way. It's fun. Skating's fun. It's a great time to come together with people who also love it.

Q: Can you tell me a bit about your book (titled "Stronger Than She Thinks")? When did that come out?

A: It came out about two and a half years ago. That was my latest book and first children's book I did. "Stronger Than She Thinks" is sort of a motto that I live by. After going through everything I went through, it's made me realize I'm stronger than I think, and I'm not special. We're all people. We all have this reservoir of strength just in case we need it, and hopefully people don't need it, to dig deep, but we have the capability to do so much more than we even typically tap into. So, it's good to know we have it. A belief in yourself is something very helpful, I think, when you're doing any sport or anything that you love — remembering why you do it, because you love it. That helps to make it easier, so if you can find passion in what you're doing, it definitely makes it not work. It was so fun to write a children's book and come down, having to narrow down an idea. That was the hardest part (to figure out) — what was a turning point so that kids and skaters could relate? It was a fun process.

Q: I'm wondering what you think of the state of figure skating today, like if you had any skaters you really enjoyed watching in the Winter Olympics? (held earlier this year in Milan, Italy)

A: The whole U.S. team was amazing, working together and having some camaraderie, not just with their own team, but with other teams across the world. It was so nice to see. I think we had that way back when I was competing, but it wasn't as shown by the press. I definitely was friends with people from all over and still am friends with them today. It's nice that that's being shown, and I think there's a reason for it. Like, you're competitors, but at the same time, you see someone doing something good, you should be able to have respect for that. This is hard and we know how hard it is, so if someone else is doing something great, celebrate that. Let it not get you afraid or nervous, let it inspire you to make your own skating better. Instead of being more at each other, it's nice to see that camaraderie with the whole team at the Olympics. It was so fun, and just the joy they brought to everyone watching was amazing.

Q: What did you think of Alysa Liu's gold medal performance?

A: Exactly that — it was joyful. She just made people smile, like I just smiled the whole time. It was fun to watch her, and you don't always feel like that in a competition. It was great.

Q: Have you been to Palm Springs and the Coachella Valley in the past? Or is this a first?

A: No, I've come here before. My husband's been in the tennis business forever, so I've come to watch the tennis before. It's amazing — the views with the mountains. It's so beautiful. I'd love to come back and hike some of them. It looks gorgeous. And the sky last night was unbelievable. It was crazy. The clouds were so interesting, stuff I've never seen. It's a beautiful place. I'm glad to be here.

Tom Coulter is a reporter for The Desert Sun. Reach him at thomas.coulter@desertsun.com.

articles.body:
The home of the Chicago Cubs became the home to some of college volleyball's top teams on Sunday.

Wrigley Field hosted volleyball matches between No. 3 Kentucky, No. 13 Penn State, No. 1 Nebraska and Missouri for the Big Ten/SEC Volleyball Challenge.

There were some hiccups in the outdoor matches, though, like the court having to be wiped down because of the humidity in Chicago. The match between Nebraska and Missouri was later suspended.

Earlier this year, teams played in the Spikes Under the Lights tournament at AT&T Stadium, which is home to the Dallas Cowboys. Nebraska's Memorial Stadium also hosted a volleyball match in 2023 that drew a historic crowd .

This is not the first time Wrigley Field has hosted college sporting event. It has been home to both college football and college hockey games in recent years.

articles.title: Hockey World Cup high over, India women chase gold at Asian Games
articles.summary: Hockey News: BENGALURU: Barely a week after finishing fifth at the FIH World Cup in Belgium, Salima Tete and her teammates were back at the SAI South Centre here, .
articles.body: BENGALURU: Barely a week after finishing fifth at the FIH World Cup in Belgium, Salima Tete and her teammates were back at the SAI South Centre here, preparing for their biggest assignment of the year — the Asian Games starting in Japan on Sept 19.With little time between the two competitions, the Indian women’s hockey team has hardly had a chance to savour or celebrate an impressive World Cup campaign. “I just got a text from a friend asking about the celebrations, given we did well at the World Cup. But the celebrations have to wait. We can enjoy afterwards. Things are going very fast, and we have to move on to the next one,” chief coach Sjoerd Marijne said.The focus now, the Dutchman added, is on building on their World Cup performance. “We paused and reflected on what we achieved. I told the girls to be very proud of what we’ve done. But we need to go further and do better than at the World Cup. What we did there may not be enough at the Asian Games. They need to stay focused,” he said.Striker Lalremsiami summed up the intensity of the turnaround, revealing that the players have not even had time for a cheat meal since returning to training. “We can’t afford to have a cheatmeal day now,” she quipped.India won bronze at the previous edition of the Asian Games and had to take the qualifier route to secure their place at the Paris Olympics. This time, with an Olympic berth for the 2028 Los Angeles Games at stake, nothing less than gold will be the target.“I know the expectations are higher. We are a very strong contender for gold. But before the gold medal, we need to win other matches. That’s why we must give our best every day. Of course, you go into a tournament to achieve the highest reward, and that is an Olympic berth,” Marijne said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Maica García: "Nunca imaginé que tener una hija pudiera marcar el final de mi etapa en Sabadell"
articles.standfirst: La internacional denuncia que "desde que fui madre el club sabía mi deseo de seguir compitiendo (...), pero ha estimado que mi carrera en el Sabadell no podía tener continuidad"
articles.summary: La internacional denuncia que "desde que fui madre el club sabía mi deseo de seguir compitiendo (...), pero ha estimado que mi carrera en el Sabadell no podía tener continuidad"
articles.body: Maica García, que fue madre en septiembre del pasado año, ha escrito este lunes en sus Redes un mensaje en el que admitió que "decir que mi etapa en el Sabadell ha terminado no es fácil". En un comunicado en redes sociales, la internacional, campeona olímpica en París 2024 y subcampeona olímpica en Londres 2012 y Tokio 2020, denuncia que "desde que tenía 4 años, el club Sabadell ha sido mi casa. Aquí aprendí a nadar, a competir, a ganar a perder... (...). Hace poco más de 11 meses fui madre. Desde entonces el club conoce mi deseo de seguir compitiendo, compatibilizando mi vida como madre y deportista (...). Sin embargo, el club ha considerado que mi carrera en el Sabadell no podía tener continuidad". La jugadora hace hincapié en que "no estoy de acuerdo con cómo se ha gestionado mi situación ni con la decisión tomada. Después de tantos años de entrega, de trabajo y de compromiso, esperaba poder cerrar mi etapa profesional en el Sabadell". Maica deja claro que "no escribo esto desde el rencor. Lo escribo desde la tristeza de tener que cerrar una etapa que jamás imaginé que terminaría así. Quiero dar las gracias a todas las personas que han formado parte de este camino (...). Me voy orgullosa de lo que hemos conseguido juntas. Pero también me voy siendo madre. Y quizás esa sea la parte más importante de todo esto. Porque después de haber dado tanto por mi deporte, nunca imaginé que tener una hija pudiera marca el final de mi etapa deportiva en el Sabadell de esta manera". El de Maica García no ha sido el único embarazo de una jugadora del Sabadell en los últimos años. De hecho, Judith Forca dio a luz unos meses antes que su compañera y estas gestaciones llevaron al CN Sabadell a pedir cambios en las reglas. Al no haber precedentes, no estaba contemplado que pudiera fichar para cubrir las bajas por maternidad. Desde la pasada temporada, los clubes pueden fichar fuera de las ventanas de mercado gracias a estos dos casos. Ya entonces Maica pedía que esas ayudas de las instituciones se extendieran también el segundo año, no sólo el primero, una vez que las jugadoras ya habían sido madres. Hace décadas, la maternidad suponía el final de la carrera para las deportistas de élite, muchas de las cuales retrasaban el momento de ser madres. Sin embargo, eso ha evolucionado y ahora hay muchos casos de deportistas que afrontan la maternidad en plena carrera deportiva y regresan después con grandes éxitos, como la atleta Ana Peleteiro, las palistas Teresa Portela y Maialen Chourraut o la nadadora Ona Carbonell. Sin embargo, y pese a los pasos que se han dado hacia adelante, la conciliación es una de las asignaturas pendientes en la sociedad en general, y en el deporte de élite en particular. De ahí que se hayan creado distintos departamentos y comisiones, como la Comisión de Maternidad y Deporte del Comité Olímpico Español, presidida por Ona Carbonell, que vela por visibilizar, asesorar y mejorar la conciliación y el apoyo a las deportistas durante su etapa maternal. Pese a todo, muchas deportistas denuncian que clubes o equipos penalizan a la deportista que decide ser madre. Una de las últimas que denunció su caso fue la ciclista Sandra Alonso, que se quedó sin equipo cuando afrontó su maternidad. Ahora, sin embargo, ha podido volver al pelotón profesional con el Laboral Kutxa.

articles.title: Pichardo, crítico con el Ultimate: "No es bueno para nuestro deporte. Dejen de excluirnos"
articles.standfirst: El saltador cuestionó la decisión de World Athletics de no incluir el triple en la nueva competición que se disputa esta fin de semana: "No entiendo cuál es su problema"
articles.summary: El saltador cuestionó la decisión de World Athletics de no incluir el triple en la nueva competición que se disputa esta fin de semana: "No entiendo cuál es su problema"
articles.body: Pedro Pichardo, campeón olímpico y mundial de triple, se mostró muy crítico con World Athletics y su decisión de no incluir el triple masculino en la nueva competición organizada por la Federación Internacional, el Ultimate Championship, que se disputa este fin de semana en Budapest. Con una periodicidad de dos años y una dotación de diez millones de dólares, una cifra récord nunca antes ofrecida en el atletismo de la que cada vencedor se llevará 150.000 dólares, este evento no acogerá todas las pruebas en su primera edición y una de las que no estará es el triple masculino. "Realmente no entiendo cuál es su problema e incluso menos, que se adopte esta decisión sin dar explicaciones", admitió Pichardo en sus redes sociales. En este sentido, el portugués destacó que "esto no es atletismo, y no es bueno para nuestro deporte. Dejen de excluirnos.”

articles.title: Cuatro españoles y el relevo mixto de 4x100 en el Ultimate Championship
articles.standfirst: Quique Llopis (110 vallas), Mohamed Attaoui (800), Jaël Bestué (200) y Marta García (5.000) entran en el selecto grupo de atletas que disputarán la nueva competición en Budapest
articles.summary: Quique Llopis (110 vallas), Mohamed Attaoui (800), Jaël Bestué (200) y Marta García (5.000) entran en el selecto grupo de atletas que disputarán la nueva competición en Budapest
articles.body: World Athletics (WA) acaba de publicar las listas definitivas para el Ultimate Championship, la nueva competición a modo de 'mundial condensado' que ve la luz este fin de semana (del 11 al 13 de septiembre) en Budapest. Y entre los atletas clasificados hay cuatro españoles, amén del cuarteto mixto de 4x100, reciente medalla de bronce en el Europeo de Birmingham. Quique Llopis (110 vallas), Mohamed Attaoui (800), Jaël Bestué (200) y Marta García (5.000) defenderán los colores patrios en un campeonato de nuevo cuño que se disputará en los años pares, para no coincidir con los Mundiales clásicos. En total serán 381 atletas de 65 federaciones los que competirán en la capital húngara. Lo harán en 28 pruebas diferentes durante tres apasionantes y condensadas jornadas con apenas tres horas de duración, a modo de reunión de la Diamond League. Los 100, 200, 400 y 800 lisos, además de las cuatro pruebas de vallas, pasarán la criba inicial de las semifinales mientras que las demás pruebas tendrán final directa. Para garantizar la participación de las grandes estrellas, WA ofrece un premio récord de 10 millones de dólares, con 150 000 dólares para cada campeón individual, una cifra muy alta para los estándares habituales. Entre los duelos más atractivos, al menos a priori, destacan los del 800 femenino, con Audrey Werro, Keely Hodgkinson y Femke Bol en liza; el de 1.500 masculino, con el esperado cara a cara entre Josh Kerr y Jakob Ingebrigtsen con Cole Hocker e Isaac Nader como testigos, y la pértiga masculina, con Armand Duplantis y Emmanouil Karalis reviviendo una creciente rivalidad que en Bruselas no se pudo disfrutar por la lesión del sueco. En el Centro Nacional de Atletismo de Budapest, sede del Mundial en 2023, también estarán Ja’Kobe Tharp, Masai Russell y Alison dos Santos, que esta temporada han batidos los récords mundiales de 110 vallas (12.75), 100 vallas (12.09) y 400 vallas (45.80) respectivamente. Especial atención también al 400 vallas masculino, con el primer duelo a tres bandas entre Dos Santos, Karsten Warholm y Rai Benjamin desde la final del Mundial de Tokio de 2025.

articles.title: After CWG bronze, Seema Kaliramna sets sights on another step towards Olympics at Asian Games
articles.summary: More sports News: The 57.44m throw in Bhubaneswar last month did not quite match the 59.73m that Seema Kaliramna had produced two months earlier. Nor did she seem parti.
articles.body: The 57.44m throw in Bhubaneswar last month did not quite match the 59.73m that Seema Kaliramna had produced two months earlier. Nor did she seem particularly bothered by it.The Bhubaneswar competition was the World Athletics Silver Level Continental Tour meet at Kalinga Stadium on August 22, her first competition after the Commonwealth Games bronze in Glasgow.In the women's discus, Commonwealth Games champion Samantha Hall was in the field along with Thailand's Subenrat Insaeng and Brazil's Andressa de Morais. De Morais won with 58.66m, Hall threw 58.43m, Subenrat 58.33m, and Seema finished fourth with 57.44m.Her personal best had come at the National Inter-State Championships in June earlier this year, where she also crossed the Asian Games qualifying mark of 55.48m. A month later in Glasgow, she won Commonwealth Games bronze with 58.65m.Now, with the Asian Games approaching, the 27-year-old discus thrower is not putting a target distance on what comes next.“I just want to throw the discus as far as I can. Now, it can be 60, it can be 65, it can be 70 metres, sir. Now, whether I get the medal or not, that's another story, sir. I just want to do my best, sir,” Seema told Timesofindia.com in an exclusive interaction ahead of the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, which begin on September 19.The 60m mark is still to come in competition, but Seema is in no hurry to force it, in fact, she laughs off the temptation to chase it too quickly.“It's better if we progress slowly. If we progress completely, it gets a little messy.”Her coach and husband, Ravinder ‘Monu’ Kaliramna, has been working along the same lines. The plan was always to use the CWG as part of the build-up, with the Asian Games in mind.Seema's own assessment after the 57.44m throw was similarly measured.“It is not that bad. According to the Asian Games, it is good.”From 54-55m in training to 59.73mThat calmness took time to build. Seema was preparing for the World University Games after her marriage in 2019 and says she was throwing 54-55m in training. A knee injury and then COVID kept her away from competition. She continued training around the same distance but could not get the competitions she needed.Then came pregnancy and childbirth.Seema gave birth to her son Rudra in 2022. He is now four years old. She returned to competitive competition 11 months after his birth, but the period around pregnancy and childbirth had left her dealing with severe physical problems.After giving birth, Seema's physical problems became severe. She has described how her shoulder and hip had become frozen during pregnancy and how the condition worsened after delivery. Doctors told her she had severe arthritis.“At that time, I was not able to walk up to 10 meters, and I was not able to pick up my child.”At one point, she wondered whether continuing to live like that was possible.“In such a condition, a person thinks that instead of living like this, it is better not to live.”She had not simply stopped throwing, but she had to work out whether her body could return to the sport at all. Ravinder's answer was to start again, but according to her body.“My husband said that we will start the game again. We will take her according to her body, as and when the muscle develops, the arthritis will reduce.”It did.Seema returned to competition in 2024. Her competition best before motherhood had been 48.08m. She went to 57.19m in 2024, won the 2025 National Games, and then moved beyond 59m this season.Seema's return to the throwing circle was not something she worked through on her own.Ravinder was there as her coach, but he was also the person beside her through pregnancy, the arthritis that followed and the long process of getting her body ready to compete again. The two have also been working towards the same Olympic goal. For Seema, that makes it difficult to separate the two roles.“When you have a goal, when you are living a dream… we are living the same dream, so there is not much difference between us.”The support behind Seema's comebackTheir sporting set-up has also been supported by the Inspire Institute of Sport, which has provided Seema with physiotherapy, massage, travel, accommodation and other support.“We don't even have a government job, we don't even have a private job, so from physio, to massage, to travelling, accommodation, everything is done by IIS. I have got full support from IIS,” Seema said.However, there was some movement on that front recently. At a Haryana government programme in Panchkula on August 26, Seema said she was approached about a junior coach's position.For now, though, the discus remains the priority. So does Rudra, even when he is not at the stadium.Rudra will watch from home againBefore the CWG, Seema had spoken about how difficult it was to leave her son behind. In Glasgow, she won bronze and then spoke about missing him. Before she left for the CWG, Seema knew what Rudra was hoping she would bring back - a medal; and she did.He will not be travelling with her to the Asian Games either.A medal will make the trip back home again, just as it did after the CWG. Seema hopes that, one day, Rudra will be the one travelling to competitions - and that she and Monu will be the ones going with him.“He cannot go with me now, but we will make him [raise him in a way] so that in the future he goes out and we go with him.”For now, Rudra will again watch from home, and Seema will go back into the circle, with a CWG bronze behind her, a 59.73m personal best beside her name and an Asian Games medal somewhere ahead.And she is already thinking beyond that. After winning at Glasgow, her first reaction was not about the distance or the podium. Instead, it was: “We did it.”Now she wants the Asian Games to be another step. “So, we will climb one more step towards the Olympics after winning a medal at the Asian Games.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Indian Olympic Association set for governance reset ahead of December polls
articles.summary: Off the field News: NEW DELHI: The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) will convene a Special General Body Meeting (SGBM) on Tuesday to adopt its amended constitution in lin.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) will convene a Special General Body Meeting (SGBM) on Tuesday to adopt its amended constitution in line with the national sports governance act, 2025, in what is set to be a significant constitutional exercise for the apex Olympic body ahead of its elections, which sees the first four-year term of P T Usha-led executive committee (EC) coming to an end later this year.The SGBM will formally adopt the constitution, paving the way for its eventual ratification by the IOA General Body in the coming months. The exercise assumes significance with the IOA's current executive term ending in Dec 2026 and elections having to be conducted under the new governance framework.All affiliated national sports federations (NSFs) and State Olympic Associations (SOAs) are expected to attend the meeting, scheduled ahead of the official send-off ceremony for the Indian contingent for the Asian Games on the same day. The meeting will bring together the IOA's members to discuss and adopt the constitutional provisions required under the new law.The amendments are necessary before the IOA can proceed with its election process. Football, athletics and cycling are among the early NSFs to have already amended their constitutions in line with the Act, sources said.The SGBM will also assume importance in the process of appointing the Returning Officer (RO) for the IOA elections. The constitutional changes need to be adopted and subsequently ratified so that the election machinery can be put in place under the new statutory framework, with the polls required to be held on or before December 10.Selected provisions of the Act came into force on Jan 1, 2026. While several federations have begun aligning their constitutions, some are finding the exercise difficult. A key challenge is the requirement for executive committees to have no more than 15 members, with some federations struggling to restructure their existing bodies accordingly. articles.summary: Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall decides to end her 2026 season after suffering "severe concussion" in a car crash and she will now miss this week's World Athletics Ultimate Championship.
articles.body:
Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall has decided to end her 2026 season after suffering "severe concussion" in a car crash.

The decision means the 27-year-old American will miss this week's World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Hungary.

"This one hurts. I'm sad, disappointed and just hurt by all of it," wrote Davis-Woodhall on social media. , external "I know this has to be part of my story.

"There has to be a reason for this. I'll never questions God's path for me. I will be back. Just a hitch in my giddy-up."

Davis-Woodhall won long jump gold at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, before topping the podium at the Worlds in Tokyo a year later.

Afterwards, she said her injuries were not life-threatening but that both cars, which were going at about 20mph, were written off.

The World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Hungary starts on 11 September, with athletes competing for a top prize of £111,000.

The competition brings together Olympic, world and Diamond League champions, as well as the year's leading performers in a three-day end-of-season event.

articles.body: La exjugadora navarra de balonmano Silvia Ederra, que fue internacional con España, ha fallecido a los 43 años tras una larga enfermedad. Natural de Estella-Lizarra, Ederra comenzó su carrera en el Itxako y jugó en clubes como Mar Alicante, Castro Urdiales, Sporting La Rioja o Bera Bera. articles.title: El Barça alza el telón de la nueva Champions ante el debutante Aarhus
articles.standfirst: El vigente campeón abre la competición que estrena formato con 24 clubes en una primera fase con seis grupos de cuatro equipos cada uno de ellos
articles.summary: El vigente campeón abre la competición que estrena formato con 24 equipos en una primera fase con seis grupos
articles.body: El vigente campeón de Europa, el Barça, alzará este miércoles (20:45 CET) el telón de la nueva Liga de Campeones en el Palau Blaugrana, donde recibirá al SAH Aarhus danés, debutante en la máxima competición continental, en el estreno de un formato que amplía la competición hasta los 24 equipos. Después de tocar el cielo en Colonia y conquistar su decimotercera corona europea, el conjunto azulgrana afronta una primera fase inédita, con seis grupos de cuatro equipos y doble vuelta. Los dos primeros clasificados de cada grupo accederán a la ronda principal, que mantendrá el formato de dos grupos de seis equipos. El nuevo curso ya ha comenzado con dos títulos para el equipo dirigido por Carlos Ortega. El Barça conquistó la Supercopa de Cataluña y, este pasado sábado, la Supercopa Ibérica por quinta vez en las cinco ediciones disputadas, después de imponerse al Sporting CP (39-34). Sin embargo, como viene siendo habitual, la verdadera medida de las aspiraciones azulgranas llegará en la máxima competición europea. "Todavía tenemos ganas de ganar", aseguró el técnico azulgrana Carlos Ortega, consciente de que el Barça afronta una temporada en la que volverá a partir entre los favoritos. "Los campeones son los campeones y todo el mundo quiere ganar, es el escaparate del balonmano mundial y todo el mundo quiere hacerlo bien", apuntó. El estreno continental también permitirá al Palau conocer de cerca a las dos únicas incorporaciones de una plantilla que mantiene buena parte del bloque campeón, aunque con dos bajas de peso como las del central esloveno Domen Makuc y el portero danés Emil Nielsen. El central Janus Smarason y el guardameta Sergey Hernández son las caras nuevas del proyecto. "Hemos fichado los mejores jugadores dentro de las mejores posibilidades que tenemos y estoy muy contento con el rendimiento de ambos", comentó el preparador culé. El meta internacional, que no pudo disputar la Supercopa Ibérica al contar con permiso del club por el inminente nacimiento de su primer hijo, regresará a la convocatoria para estrenarse ante su nueva afición. El islandés, por su parte, tendrá también su primera gran noche europea con la camiseta azulgrana. Sobre el papel, el estreno se presenta propicio para un Barça que llega en un buen momento de forma y que ha demostrado en este inicio de temporada que mantiene intactas sus señas de identidad. El conjunto azulgrana parte como claro favorito ante un rival que se estrena en la 'Champions', pero Ortega advirtió del riesgo de confiarse y calificó el encuentro como "un partido de trampa". El Skanderborg Aarhus accede a la máxima competición continental después de beneficiarse de la tercera plaza concedida por la Federación Europea a Dinamarca. La pasada temporada disputó la Liga Europea y cayó en la ronda de eliminatorias ante el SG Flensburg alemán. El conjunto danés mantiene buena parte del núcleo de la pasada campaña y cuenta con varios argumentos para intentar incomodar al vigente campeón de Europa. Entre ellos destaca el lateral derecho islandés Kristjan Kristjansson, máximo goleador del equipo el pasado curso. Bajo palos, el rendimiento de Magnus Petersen puede resultar determinante. El joven meta danés ya dejó muestras de su capacidad la pasada temporada, cuando ante el Granollers superó el 40% de paradas en la primera parte en la victoria del conjunto nórdico por 26-31.

articles.title: ‘Back to blue’: Hockey India reverses saffron jersey decision for Asian Games after World Cup uproar
articles.summary: Hockey News: NEW DELHI: Hockey India has seemingly reversed its controversial decision to make saffron the Indian hockey teams’ primary colour, with both the men’s.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Hockey India has seemingly reversed its controversial decision to make saffron the Indian hockey teams’ primary colour, with both the men’s and women’s sides set to return to their traditional blue jerseys at the upcoming Asian Games in Japan.The decision comes just weeks after the saffron kits became a major talking point at the FIH Hockey World Cup in the Netherlands and Belgium. Hockey India had switched from its long-standing blue jersey to saffron ahead of the tournament, citing technical concerns over visibility against the blue playing surface.However, the change sparked criticism from several former India captains and also triggered an internal controversy within the federation. Now, as the teams prepare for the Asian Games, blue will once again be the first-choice colour, with saffron retained as the secondary option.“Indian Olympic Association (IOA) asked us our preferred choice of kit and HI has given the first preference as blue, with the secondary colour being saffron,” Hockey India treasurer Shekar Manoharan said on Tuesday.Saffron switch sparked uproarHockey India had announced the change on July 27, arguing that the decision was based on feedback from players and coaches. According to the federation, blue jerseys against the blue turf could affect on-field visibility, while yellow and orange had emerged as possible alternatives.Saffron was ultimately selected because of its association with the Indian national flag.The move, however, quickly became controversial. Former India captains including Pargat Singh, Dhanraj Pillay, Ajit Pal Singh and Viren Rasquinha questioned the decision to move away from a colour that had long been associated with Indian hockey.The debate intensified when Hockey India president Dilip Tirkey revealed through an internal communication that he had not been consulted over the change. Tirkey made it clear that his objection was not necessarily to saffron itself, but to the manner in which the decision was taken without being placed before the federation’s elected leadership and Executive Board.The issue also spilled into the political arena, with former Odisha chief minister Naveen Patnaik criticising the move and alleging that the change was politically motivated.India's World Cup campaign did little to silence the debate over the technical justification. The men's team finished eighth after two wins in six matches, while the women's side produced India's best-ever finish at the tournament, securing fifth place.Blue returns with Olympic qualification at stakeThe return to blue comes at a crucial tournament for both teams. The Asian Games will carry added significance as India seeks qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya held a review meeting with the two teams' coaches, captains and Hockey India officials and urged them to put the World Cup campaigns behind them and focus on the Olympic qualification challenge.The Harmanpreet Singh-led men's side will enter the Asian Games as defending champions and chase an unprecedented fifth gold medal. The women's team, meanwhile, will be aiming to end a 44-year wait for an Asian Games title after finishing third in the 2022 edition.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Teddy Riner, Olympic judo legend, to miss another World Championships
articles.summary: Teddy Riner lit the 2024 Olympic cauldron with Marie-Jose Perec.
articles.body:
France's Teddy Riner, the most successful judoka in Olympic history, will miss a second consecutive World Championships due to injury, further delaying his return to major competition for the first time since the Paris Games.

Riner, 37, will miss October's World Championships in Baku, Azerbaijan, due to a shoulder injury, according to French media citing the French judo federation.

"There's a small piece of bone loose in his shoulder, and that's what's causing the sensitivity," said Riner's trainer, Julien Corvo, according to a translation of an Agence-France Presse report . "Since we're not in a rush, we wanted to do some competitions before the World Championships. That wasn't possible because of this, so obviously we can't go straight into a World Championship.

"But it's not serious. It's just that the timing isn't right. When he raises his arm, he feels a sort of small electric shock. The medical staff said it's not serious in itself, but of course, we need to give it time."

Riner also missed the 2025 World Championships as he worked his way back from elbow surgery, prioritizing long-term preparation for a record sixth Olympic bid at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

Riner owns the most Olympic gold medals (five) and medals (seven) in judo history, including individual heavyweight titles in 2012, 2016 and 2024.

He also shared the honor of lighting the Paris Olympic cauldron with fellow Guadeloupe native Marie-José Pérec, a track star from the 1990s.

Since winning individual and team gold in Paris, Riner has repeatedly said that he plans to compete through LA 2028.

"Now that I have become the record holder in my sport, I experience things differently," he said in April 2025, according to a translation of a L'Equipe report . "Now, four years (before the 2028 Olympics), I will try to go moonwalking in Los Angeles. No pressure, only pleasure. And if I manage to go and collect a fourth (individual) gold medal, I will do it with joy. That is the objective. But it is certain that there will not be the pressure that I was subjected to in Tokyo, in Paris. Now, it is above all pleasure. And to live the last four years of my sport at the top. And to finish in 2029 to say goodbye."

He is already the oldest Olympic judo gold medalist, and in LA can become the oldest judoka to win an Olympic medal of any color, according to Olympedia.

Riner also owns the record of most world championship titles in judo — 12 from 2009 through 2023, including two in separate open competitions without weight categories and one in a team event.

He also skipped World Championships in both the Tokyo and Paris Olympic cycles.

The Los Angeles Olympics, with a record 353 medal events, open July 14, 2028.

articles.title: Dilip Gavit's inspirational journey: From losing his right arm at five after a tree fall to raising the tricolour on podiums
articles.summary: More sports News: NEW DELHI: At five, Dilip Mahadu Gavit knew little about the fragility of life. A fall from a tree left him with a serious injury to his right arm, bu.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: At five, Dilip Mahadu Gavit knew little about the fragility of life. A fall from a tree left him with a serious injury to his right arm, but there was no reason to believe that a childhood accident would alter the course of his life. The wound initially appeared manageable, but it turned septic. What followed was every parent's nightmare. Doctors had no choice but to amputate his arm.For most, losing an arm at such a tender age could have meant the end of dreams before they had even begun. For Gavit, it became the beginning of a battle he would spend years fighting, one that would eventually take him to a place few could have imagined: the Commonwealth Games podium. Earlier this year in Glasgow, the 23-year-old won gold in the men's 100m T47 final in 10.71 seconds, a Commonwealth Games record, and became the first Indian male para-athlete to win gold at the Games.For Gavit, though, the medal's significance ran deeper than the timing or the record. He credited his medal to Vaijnath Kale, the coach who spotted Gavit's potential when he was still a boy competing in local races in Maharashtra."The first thing that comes to my mind is that the day of my event was Guru Purnima. So, in a way, I gave my guru his gurudakshina that day. That makes me feel very good, and it is something I will always remember," Gavit told TimesofIndia.com on the sidelines of an event organised by (SBI) Life Insurance.Gavit's CWG final was no textbook 100m victory. His start wasn't the strongest, and by halfway, he looked to be chasing the race rather than controlling it. The explosive runners had established their advantage, while Gavit leaned on qualities built through years of 400m training. As others began to lose momentum, Gavit kept coming. His speed endurance became his advantage. He ate into the gap in the final 40 metres, moved past the runners ahead of him and crossed the line in 10.71 seconds. The Commonwealth Games record was gone, and so was any doubt about whether a 400m athlete could make a serious impact over 100m.For Gavit, it also vindicated the decision to pursue the event after the 400m was left off the programme. Even after producing the biggest 100m performance of his career, though, he knows there's still work to do.The guru who shaped Gavit's careerGavit grew up in Tora Dongri, a tribal hamlet in Nashik, where sporting infrastructure was scarce and opportunities were limited. Gavit used to compete in races at school even when facilities and resources weren't readily available, and his willingness to compete eventually brought him to Kale's attention. Kale, a corporate employee turned coach, was impressed with Gavit and requested his parents to let him train, but due to the family's financial difficulties, he didn't get the green light. Kale was confident that he had found a special talent, and he virtually adopted Dilip.What followed was more than a conventional coach-athlete relationship. Kale took Gavit into his home and gave him the environment he needed to pursue athletics. For a boy from a village with little access to sport, it changed the trajectory of his life. Gavit has never forgotten it."I come from a small village where there aren't many facilities, especially when it comes to sport. To take me from there and keep me at his home is something not many people would do. He did that for me. For me, he has been like God," he reminisced.The switch from 400m to 100m in GlasgowKale began moulding him primarily as a 400m runner, an event that demands far more than raw speed. A successful one-lap athlete has to understand pace, conserve energy through the middle stages, and still have enough left to attack the final 100m.Gavit's progress soon took him beyond para-athletics. Gavit competed in open competitions, regularly holding his own against able-bodied athletes. He reached the Under-20 400m final at the open nationals in 2021 and was part of Maharashtra's bronze-medal 4x400m relay team at the 2022 Khelo India Youth Games.His move into international para-athletics took him to the 2022 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, where he won 400m gold, establishing him as one of India's leading para sprinters. Glasgow would require something different, and interestingly, he did not arrive at the 2026 Commonwealth Games as a 100m specialist. If one event defined the youngster, it was the 400m.On a wet track in Glasgow, though, it was the shortest sprint that gave him the biggest moment of his career. He wasn't among the leaders for much of the race. The pure sprinters' explosiveness had put him behind early, but things changed in the closing stages. Drawing on the speed endurance he has built as a 400m runner, Gavit surged through the final stretch and swept past his rivals.The absence of the 400m from the Commonwealth Games programme left Gavit with a choice. Rather than miss the Games altogether, he turned to the 100m, an event he was already running as part of his preparation for the longer sprint. The shift wasn't as sudden as it may have looked from outside. Kale had been preparing him for the 100m for years."The preparation for the 100m did not start this year. It has actually been going on for the last four years," Kale told this website. "As you saw, he competed in the 100m at the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou. He reached the quarter-finals and semi-finals, but unfortunately, he fouled in the final and was disqualified."That foul stayed with Gavit. He'd already won a 400m medal at those Asian Games, but the 100m disappointment bothered him. "My coach had actually started preparing me for the 100m much earlier, in 2022. At the Asian Games, I fouled in the 100m, so I could not finish the event. I won a medal in the 400m there, but I still felt bad about the 100m because of the foul," he said.That made Glasgow personal. "So when I won the Commonwealth Games gold in the 100m, it felt really good," he added.There was a practical reason for the switch too. "We have been training for both events in parallel. Since the 400m was not part of the Commonwealth Games programme, we focused on qualifying for and competing in the 100m," Kale explained.'Still a 400m runner'The irony of Gavit's CWG triumph is that despite winning one of the most prestigious sprint titles in Indian para-athletics, Kale doesn't see him as a 100m specialist. "He is still primarily a 400m athlete. But his performance in the 100m has also been very good," Kale said.The 100m and 400m are both sprint events, but the demands differ fundamentally: one is a battle for explosive acceleration and maximum velocity, while the other is about combining speed with the ability to sustain it over an entire lap."The 100m is a sprint and demands speed, while the 400m is a speed-endurance event. Balancing the two is quite difficult, but fortunately, we have been managing both very well, and the results have also been very good."Gavit sees the difference clearly himself. "In the 400m, the focus is much greater because you have to plan the entire race. You have to know how to run the first 100m, how to maintain your pace through the middle of the race and then give everything you have in the final stretch," he said."In the 100m, you just have to run hard and the race is over quickly. I actually enjoy the 100m because it finishes so quickly."There's something amusing in that: the athlete who has just conquered the Commonwealth 100m is still happiest thinking of himself as a 400m runner, while his coach tries to make sure both versions of Gavit keep developing.The laurels he wants nextGavit believes the Glasgow conditions cost him something. "The climate there was not very good, and because of that, my start was a little slow. That is something I want to improve."A Commonwealth gold and a Games record might have been enough for most athletes to sit back and enjoy. Gavit is already looking at the next benchmark. "I want to break the Commonwealth Games record again in 2030."Before then comes a more immediate challenge. The Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya will demand that Gavit quickly switch gears from 100m preparation back to the 400m, and after two months of concentrating heavily on the shorter sprint, Kale knows the transition won't be straightforward."It is definitely a little difficult at the moment because our entire focus has been on the 100m for the last two months. Now, suddenly, we have to shift our focus back towards the 400m. So there are some challenges." But the target is clear. "There is no doubt that we will give our best, and our commitment will be to win medals for India in both events."Gavit wants more than medals. He wants gold in both. "At the next Asian Games, I want to compete in both the 100m and 400m and win gold in both."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: PT Usha-led IOA forms panel to probe sexual harassment allegations against Hockey India secretary
articles.summary: Hockey News: NEW DELHI: The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) has formed a four-member independent inquiry committee to investigate the sexual harassment allegation.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) has formed a four-member independent inquiry committee to investigate the sexual harassment allegations made against Hockey India secretary Bhola Nath Singh by former India women's hockey captain Asunta Lakra.The committee has been set up following a directive from the Union sports ministry. It will be headed by retired high court judge Deepa Sharma, with former track and field athlete Vandana Rao, former India women's hockey captain Mamta Kharb, and lawyer Sitwat Nabi as members.Lakra, who is also a member of Hockey India's Executive Board, has accused Singh of threatening and harassing her after she objected to the alleged sexual harassment of girls in Jharkhand by local coach Sudhir Golla.The IOA has directed Hockey India to bear all expenses related to the inquiry committee, including honorarium, travel, accommodation and other incidental costs."Hockey India is also requested to extend its full cooperation to the committee and to ensure that all relevant documents, information and such other assistance as may be required is made available to the committee in a timely manner...," IOA president PT Usha's letter to Hockey India stated, as quoted by news agency PTI.The dispute between Lakra and Hockey India has also led to a separate inquiry by the federation's ethics committee.Hockey India's ethics committee issued a show-cause notice to Lakra and started an inquiry after young player Albela Rani Toppo accused the former captain of threatening and intimidating her. Toppo, who is also from Jharkhand, alleged that Lakra threatened to end her career for unspecified reasons.Lakra rejected Hockey India's action and called it "continued intimidation and retaliation". She appealed to sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya to intervene and stop the ethics committee inquiry against her.The sports ministry had earlier asked the IOA to set up an independent panel to investigate Lakra's allegations of sexual harassment against the Hockey India secretary.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
